Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images US officials focus on identification and rapid action as measles cases rise Authorities in Delaware tackle cluster with vaccination and contact tracing – but field has been weakened by cuts Measles outbreaks are igniting throughout the United States as the nation passes the highest case count in 30 years – putting greater pressure on state and local health departments and highlighting the importance of early identification and quick action. The US has officially surpassed last year’s tally of measles cases, reaching 2,371 confirmed infections by the end of July. Those numbers have been driven by clusters in Arizona, South Carolina, and Utah – but in times of high transmission, outbreaks elsewhere become more likely. And with decreasing vaccination rates across the country, these sparks are falling on increasingly dry timber. In July, Delaware announced its first case of measles in more than a decade. Two days later, officials declared an outbreak, with five known cases. Like other parts of the country, vaccination rates have dropped in Delaware, from 98.5% of kindergartners vaccinated against measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) in 2016 compared to 94.1% now. A threshold of about 95% is considered essential for herd immunity to protect those who cannot get vaccinated or who don’t mount a good immune reaction – including babies and cancer patients. “We don’t want to be below that threshold. And the lower we get, the more likelihood there is that someone who can’t be vaccinated yet – because of their age or because of their immune status – is going to come into contact with someone who has unfortunately contracted measles,” said Robert Rosenbaum, Delaware’s medical director for emergency medical services and preparedness. Attitudes toward vaccines have changed in a couple of different ways, he said. The idea of a link between autism and vaccination, now disproved by multiple studies, proved to be “horrible misinformation” that “created a lot of confusion for people”, Rosenbaum said. Some parents also began trying to create their own vaccination schedule out of the belief that children receive too many vaccines – a view frequently espoused by Donald Trump. The pandemic supercharged existing misinformation about vaccines. “There were a lot of people who had feelings about the Covid vaccination, and that has crossed over to other vaccinations where people are moving away from everything,” Rosenbaum said. William Chasanov, an infectious disease physician at Beebe Healthcare in Lewes, Delaware, said he “did see the pendulum swing with Covid”. The Covid vaccines saved hundreds of thousands of lives – but at the same time, more of the public began seeing vaccines as optional, he said. “There was a shift in thought that ‘maybe I don’t need vaccines for things that I haven’t seen,’” Chasanov said. The measles vaccine has in some ways become a victim of its own success; those who haven’t encountered measles before don’t understand why it needs to be prevented, he said. Robert F Kennedy Jr, now the health secretary, spent about two decades spreading misinformation about vaccines – and that advocacy went into overtime during the pandemic, when wider audiences were exposed to his anti-vaccine views. As health secretary, Kennedy has framed measles vaccination during this outbreak as a personal choice, and he has falsely claimed it’s “very difficult” for healthy children to die of measles. But the evidence strongly points to the effectiveness and safety of two doses of the MMR vaccines, Rosenbaum said. “Anyone who isn’t advocating that is not following science consistently.” Vaccines are key to prevent measles – but equally important is education for families who have questions about vaccines and access to healthcare for those who need the shots and other care, experts said. Measles is an awful disease, Chasanov said. It can bring high fevers, difficulty breathing, and extreme lethargy. It can infect the brain, causing encephalitis, which can have lasting health effects. And it can lead to death – even, sometimes, years later. “Understanding what the consequences could be is part of that education,” Chasanov said. “And it’s important to know that the measles vaccine is one of the most highly effective vaccines that we’ve had on the market for decades ... Measles is highly contagious, but it’s also highly preventable.” The day after the first case was announced in Delaware, more than 60 people received MMR vaccinations at public health clinics and mobile vaccination units. “When things hit closer to home, you start asking questions because it becomes more personal,” Chasanov said. “It spurs a healthy conversation that I encourage people to have with their clinicians to say, ‘Do I need to do anything different with vaccination?’” Anyone born before 1989 may need to get a second dose of the measles shot, which became standard practice in the late 80s. One measles shot is about 93% effective, but two are about 97% effective. Those born before 1957 likely have immunity from measles infection as a child. At this point, public health officials aren’t recommending early vaccination for children under one or children under four who have only received one shot – unless they’re in contact with a positive patient. “What we don’t have at this point is a large-scale epidemic where we might be changing some of those vaccine recommendations,” Rosenbaum said. “Certainly, if the numbers change or for some indication to change it, we would revisit that.” Delaware has released few details about the cases for medical privacy reasons. The first four patients were all unvaccinated men in Kent county. The fifth patient was vaccinated and has extremely mild symptoms – one of the benefits of vaccination. An outbreak is declared when three or more connected cases appear. “Delaware has responded very rapidly,” Chasanov said. The division of public health met with healthcare systems and providers to walk through plans in case someone with measles walks through their doors. Officials are approaching the outbreak with a two-pronged approach: vaccination and contact tracing, the mainstays of public health. The field, however, has been battered – by the long hours and stress of the pandemic, and by chronic underfunding and growing threats that stretch public health thin. Contact tracing is how officials discovered the four additional cases. After the first person tested positive, public health staff got in touch with anyone who was in contact with him – searching especially for very high-risk people like young children (and anyone else) not vaccinated yet or only partially immunized, pregnant people, and anyone with a weakened immune response. “The contact tracing has really done a nice job of identifying the at-risk contacts,” Rosenbaum said. “So the good news is, I would say, if people haven’t heard from us, we’re not actively looking for them.” Now, they’re monitoring contacts to see if they develop symptoms, and they’re looking for any other cases they may have missed in contact tracing. They’re also trying to reach anyone with poor access to healthcare, including those without health insurance. ”The public health safety net is an important one,” Rosenbaum said. “We don’t want anyone who wants to get vaccinated to feel like they’re unable to do so because of insurance status ... That’s the function of public health, right? To help people who are at risk and may be vulnerable.” Outbreaks like these are happening all over the country, with pockets of cases sprouting up and officials racing to prevent spread through early identification, contact tracing, vaccination, education, and improved healthcare access. “We have a process that we follow,” Rosenbaum said. “And when we follow that process well, we have the opportunity to stem the outbreak.” Explore more on these topics US healthcare news Share Reuse this content Most viewed California woman who admitted to stabbing wife had also killed husband Trump’s favorite cable news channel is pushing back against his war on Iran ‘It didn’t need to end this way’: mother of US teen trafficked and killed decries police failures ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy Cambridge academics reject university’s attempt to end row over Jason Arday Most viewed Most viewed

Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images US officials focus on identification and rapid action as measles cases rise Authorities in Delaware tackle cluster with vaccination and contact tracing – but field has been weakened by cuts Measles outbreaks are igniting throughout the United States as the nation passes the highest case count in 30 years – putting greater pressure on state and local health departments and highlighting the importance of early identification and quick action. The US has officially surpassed last year’s tally of measles cases, reaching 2,371 confirmed infections by the end of July. Those numbers have been driven by clusters in Arizona, South Carolina, and Utah – but in times of high transmission, outbreaks elsewhere become more likely. And with decreasing vaccination rates across the country, these sparks are falling on increasingly dry timber. In July, Delaware announced its first case of measles in more than a decade. Two days later, officials declared an outbreak, with five known cases. Like other parts of the country, vaccination rates have dropped in Delaware, from 98.5% of kindergartners vaccinated against measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) in 2016 compared to 94.1% now. A threshold of about 95% is considered essential for herd immunity to protect those who cannot get vaccinated or who don’t mount a good immune reaction – including babies and cancer patients. “We don’t want to be below that threshold. And the lower we get, the more likelihood there is that someone who can’t be vaccinated yet – because of their age or because of their immune status – is going to come into contact with someone who has unfortunately contracted measles,” said Robert Rosenbaum, Delaware’s medical director for emergency medical services and preparedness. Attitudes toward vaccines have changed in a couple of different ways, he said. The idea of a link between autism and vaccination, now disproved by multiple studies, proved to be “horrible misinformation” that “created a lot of confusion for people”, Rosenbaum said. Some parents also began trying to create their own vaccination schedule out of the belief that children receive too many vaccines – a view frequently espoused by Donald Trump. The pandemic supercharged existing misinformation about vaccines. “There were a lot of people who had feelings about the Covid vaccination, and that has crossed over to other vaccinations where people are moving away from everything,” Rosenbaum said. William Chasanov, an infectious disease physician at Beebe Healthcare in Lewes, Delaware, said he “did see the pendulum swing with Covid”. The Covid vaccines saved hundreds of thousands of lives – but at the same time, more of the public began seeing vaccines as optional, he said. “There was a shift in thought that ‘maybe I don’t need vaccines for things that I haven’t seen,’” Chasanov said. The measles vaccine has in some ways become a victim of its own success; those who haven’t encountered measles before don’t understand why it needs to be prevented, he said. Robert F Kennedy Jr, now the health secretary, spent about two decades spreading misinformation about vaccines – and that advocacy went into overtime during the pandemic, when wider audiences were exposed to his anti-vaccine views. As health secretary, Kennedy has framed measles vaccination during this outbreak as a personal choice, and he has falsely claimed it’s “very difficult” for healthy children to die of measles. But the evidence strongly points to the effectiveness and safety of two doses of the MMR vaccines, Rosenbaum said. “Anyone who isn’t advocating that is not following science consistently.” Vaccines are key to prevent measles – but equally important is education for families who have questions about vaccines and access to healthcare for those who need the shots and other care, experts said. Measles is an awful disease, Chasanov said. It can bring high fevers, difficulty breathing, and extreme lethargy. It can infect the brain, causing encephalitis, which can have lasting health effects. And it can lead to death – even, sometimes, years later. “Understanding what the consequences could be is part of that education,” Chasanov said. “And it’s important to know that the measles vaccine is one of the most highly effective vaccines that we’ve had on the market for decades ... Measles is highly contagious, but it’s also highly preventable.” The day after the first case was announced in Delaware, more than 60 people received MMR vaccinations at public health clinics and mobile vaccination units. “When things hit closer to home, you start asking questions because it becomes more personal,” Chasanov said. “It spurs a healthy conversation that I encourage people to have with their clinicians to say, ‘Do I need to do anything different with vaccination?’” Anyone born before 1989 may need to get a second dose of the measles shot, which became standard practice in the late 80s. One measles shot is about 93% effective, but two are about 97% effective. Those born before 1957 likely have immunity from measles infection as a child. At this point, public health officials aren’t recommending early vaccination for children under one or children under four who have only received one shot – unless they’re in contact with a positive patient. “What we don’t have at this point is a large-scale epidemic where we might be changing some of those vaccine recommendations,” Rosenbaum said. “Certainly, if the numbers change or for some indication to change it, we would revisit that.” Delaware has released few details about the cases for medical privacy reasons. The first four patients were all unvaccinated men in Kent county. The fifth patient was vaccinated and has extremely mild symptoms – one of the benefits of vaccination. An outbreak is declared when three or more connected cases appear. “Delaware has responded very rapidly,” Chasanov said. The division of public health met with healthcare systems and providers to walk through plans in case someone with measles walks through their doors. Officials are approaching the outbreak with a two-pronged approach: vaccination and contact tracing, the mainstays of public health. The field, however, has been battered – by the long hours and stress of the pandemic, and by chronic underfunding and growing threats that stretch public health thin. Contact tracing is how officials discovered the four additional cases. After the first person tested positive, public health staff got in touch with anyone who was in contact with him – searching especially for very high-risk people like young children (and anyone else) not vaccinated yet or only partially immunized, pregnant people, and anyone with a weakened immune response. “The contact tracing has really done a nice job of identifying the at-risk contacts,” Rosenbaum said. “So the good news is, I would say, if people haven’t heard from us, we’re not actively looking for them.” Now, they’re monitoring contacts to see if they develop symptoms, and they’re looking for any other cases they may have missed in contact tracing. They’re also trying to reach anyone with poor access to healthcare, including those without health insurance. ”The public health safety net is an important one,” Rosenbaum said. “We don’t want anyone who wants to get vaccinated to feel like they’re unable to do so because of insurance status ... That’s the function of public health, right? To help people who are at risk and may be vulnerable.” Outbreaks like these are happening all over the country, with pockets of cases sprouting up and officials racing to prevent spread through early identification, contact tracing, vaccination, education, and improved healthcare access. “We have a process that we follow,” Rosenbaum said. “And when we follow that process well, we have the opportunity to stem the outbreak.” Explore more on these topics US healthcare news Share Reuse this content Most viewed California woman who admitted to stabbing wife had also killed husband Trump’s favorite cable news channel is pushing back against his war on Iran ‘It didn’t need to end this way’: mother of US teen trafficked and killed decries police failures ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy Cambridge academics reject university’s attempt to end row over Jason Arday Most viewed Most viewed

(Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS) By Leif Greiss | lgreiss@mcall.com | The Morning Call PUBLISHED: August 3, 2026 at 7:52 PM EDT | UPDATED: August 6, 2026 at 3:06 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... St. Luke’s University Hospital said late Monday that it’s treating its first cases of the measles “in recent memory.” According to a health network spokesperson, the hospital was treating two children from Lehigh County. The two are siblings, and both were unvaccinated, the spokesperson said. Though both are St. Luke’s patients, one child at first visited a Lehigh Valley Health Network hospital while St. Luke’s pediatricians attended to the other child remotely. The network did not specify where in Lehigh County the siblings were from. Dr. Jennifer Janco, chair of pediatrics at St. Luke’s, said one was hospitalized but released, and both are recovering at home. Janco said the network already completed contact tracing for its networks and that there were no potential exposures at any St. Luke’s facilities. All other contract tracing is being conducted by the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Janco said that the children had traveled internationally and there were multiple potential places where they could have come in contact with measles. St. Luke’s last month warned of an eastern Pennsylvania outbreak of the highly infectious disease and encouraged parents to take extra steps to protect their children. Seventy-five infections were linked to an outbreak that began in Lebanon and Lancaster counties in late April. Two cases were reported in Berks County, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. Across the state, so far there have been 176 confirmed cases of measles in 2026, with 35 reported in the last seven days. Because of the outbreak, the Health Department is recommending infants ages 6-11 months receive an early dose of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Children who have already received one MMR dose at 1 year of age, which is the typical age the first doses are given, may be eligible to receive their second dose earlier than their fourth year, which is the usual time the second dose is given. “Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases, but vaccination is the safest and most effective way to protect your child and those around them,” Janco said. The St. Luke’s measles cases are the first known ones reported in the Lehigh Valley since 2019 . An Allentown resident at Lehigh Valley Hospital-Cedar Crest with measles marked the city’s first case in more than 20 years, officials said at the time. It caused five people who were potentially exposed to be ordered to quarantine, including one who received a rare court order to do so. There were two potential measles exposures in 2011, according to previous reporting by The Morning Call. Since the introduction and adoption of the measles vaccine in the 1960s, measles cases in the Lehigh Valley have been rare. The last known death from measles in the Lehigh Valley was a Bethlehem Township girl who died in 1991 after she contracted the disease in Philadelphia amid a major national outbreak. Later that year, six children in the Lehigh Valley got measles, as part of an outbreak that affected at least 14 children in Lehigh, Northampton, Lancaster and Lebanon counties. Before the introduction of the vaccine, measles was a serious and pervasive threat that often seriously disrupted school and everyday life. In 1912, The Morning Call reported that one child being sent to school sick with measles resulted in 12 Lehigh Valley schools temporarily closing and 14,000 students missing school to prevent exposure amid a national measles outbreak. In winter 1916, another national outbreak led to hundreds of people in Allentown getting infected with the disease and the entire city being placed under quarantine, with all schools shut down for several weeks. Yet another national epidemic of measles in 1923 led to at least 500 people in Allentown getting sick in January, February and March, and on one day in May 1923, there were 64 school children in Alburtis, nearly a third of the students in the town, who were out sick with measles. Update: LVHN was also initially involved in the treatment of one child. Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword Start solving OpinionFirst Opinion What my colleagues and I will look for as we assess U.S. measles elimination status Determining measles’ status in the U.S. is about more than just case numbers Manage alerts for this article Email this article Share this article A single virus particle, or “virion,” of measles virus, seen through a thin-section transmission electron micrograph (TEM).Cynthia S. Goldsmith, William Bellini/CDC By Noel T. Brewer Aug. 6, 2026 Brewer chairs the U.S. committee that reviews the annual CDC measles reports to verify whether the U.S. maintains or loses measles elimination status. Elimination of measles in the United States in 2000 was a landmark public health achievement. Twenty-five years later, the country has already reported more cases this year than it did in all of 2025, a stark reminder that public health victories can be reversed. In mid-August, colleagues and I will review the evidence and decide whether the U.S. has maintained measles elimination. In many ways, our roles bookend that history. Several of these colleagues helped lead the national effort that ended endemic measles transmission in 2000. And I now chair the committee that must determine whether that hard‐won status still holds — or whether the country is on the verge of losing it. Advertisement To independently certify the CDC’s annual report on measles elimination, the U.S. maintains the United States of America National Verification Committee for the Elimination of Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome. (Yes, it’s a mouthful.) After our committee’s review, we will forward the report and our expert opinion to the Regional Verification Commission of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). Then, in November, this PAHO committee will announce whether the U.S. has maintained measles elimination. Confidentiality agreements mean that I cannot share the contents of the 2026 report. But here’s what we will be looking for. A lot will be familiar. We will review measles rates for the nation. These data are public and show a runaway train. This year is about to exceed any previous year in the last third of a century, with 2,371 measles cases so far. Outbreaks are occurring in most states, with 34 new outbreaks this year alone. Utah’s outbreak, which began in June 2025, has lasted for more than a year so far. Advertisement We will look at detailed analyses of each outbreak. The largest outbreaks for the report period have spanned the continental U.S. — South Carolina and Utah, followed by Texas and Virginia. One of the most worrisome is the ongoing outbreak in Utah, which apparently has gone on for more than 12 months, the main criterion for loss of elimination. Importantly, we will look at how long the chains of transmission lasted. This is usually established with shoe-leather epidemiology. When measles cases are reported, public health workers fan out in the community to interview the various contacts and identify places they’ve been and may have exposed others. They use this narrative information to stitch together chains of transmission. They also try to prevent further cases by offering postexposure vaccination or immune globulin and quarantining people who were exposed to others with measles. What will be new in this year’s report is whole genome sequencing. In recent years, CDC had done partial genome sequencing to look at the genetic signature of the measles viruses causing the cases and try to understand their evolution, which was the best that they could do. But the technology has advanced to be more comprehensive and detailed. Whole genome sequencing allows much better resolution of transmission chains. Several states, including Utah, Arizona, and South Carolina, have already taken this approach. They uncovered signatures of unseen cases by noticing abrupt “skips” in the virus’s evolutionary trail. By relying on a central lab and standardized methods, the CDC can now track measles across state lines with far greater precision. In 2025, Canada and the U.S. used partial genome sequencing data to verify their measles elimination status. For Canada, the data were especially important. Seasonal workers brought measles from Mexico, and new cases left with them in the fall and returned with them in the spring. Partial genome sequencing did not find important differences between the fall and spring cases, something that whole genome sequencing may have allowed. PAHO was unpersuaded that these were separate introduction events, and as a result Canada lost its measles elimination status in November 2025. The U.S. and Mexico may be next. Advertisement America has been trading measles cases with Canada and Mexico during the recent outbreak. Given the ongoing transmission among the countries, it would appear that measles again became endemic in North America far before it was declared as such. The extensive and ongoing sharing of cases across borders in North America raises an interesting question of whether the definition of measles chains should end at the borders of closely linked countries. As my colleagues and I review the 2026 measles elimination report, we will marvel at the extraordinary efforts of local, regional, and federal public health to rein in these outbreaks. We will be frankly amazed at the extraordinary level of detail generated by the CDC and other public health agencies. The report will reflect cutting-edge science at the top of its game. In the end, the question that will be on our minds is: Has the U.S. lost its elimination status? Some clues appear in the U.S.’s public data. The country has had measles cases every week since January 2025. That would be 20 months of weekly measles cases at this point. Of course, maybe genomic data points will save the day. Maybe they won’t. Regardless of the outcome of our meeting and PAHO’s decision in November, the U.S. clearly has a measles problem, as do Canada and Mexico. Elimination status marks whether a country has stopped sustained domestic transmission. Losing that status would signal a consequential reversal, evidence that the systems and protections that once kept measles at bay no longer do. We can and must do more than we’re doing to end the extraordinary spread of measles in our country and beyond. The nation needs strong, positive communications to the public about the importance of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination and promotion of health care providers as trusted advisers on immunizations. A dedicated communication campaign led by the federal government would be usual in past years at this stage. These communications need clear, vocal, and regular support from the highest levels of the U.S. government. Initiatives to better understand and address vaccine hesitancy are also urgently needed. Advertisement Measles is a brutal disease that has no medical cure. Parents of children made sickest must wait it out in the hospital, despairingly wondering whether their child will die. That level of risk is indefensible in 2026 — more than 25 years after the United States achieved measles elimination. Kids are suffering and dying from a disease we already know how to prevent, and that failure is entirely ours. Noel Brewer is the Gillings distinguished professor in public health at the University of North Carolina. He chairs the U.S. committee that reviews the annual CDC measles reports to verify whether the U.S. maintains or loses measles elimination status. Letter to the editor Have an opinion on this essay? PAHO was unpersuaded that these were separate introduction events, and as a result Canada lost its measles elimination status in November 2025. The U.S. and Mexico may be next. Advertisement America has been trading measles cases with Canada and Mexico during the recent outbreak. Given the ongoing transmission among the countries, it would appear that measles again became endemic in North America far before it was declared as such. The extensive and ongoing sharing of cases across borders in North America raises an interesting question of whether the definition of measles chains should end at the borders of closely linked countries. As my colleagues and I review the 2026 measles elimination report, we will marvel at the extraordinary efforts of local, regional, and federal public health to rein in these outbreaks. We will be frankly amazed at the extraordinary level of detail generated by the CDC and other public health agencies. The report will reflect cutting-edge science at the top of its game. In the end, the question that will be on our minds is: Has the U.S. lost its elimination status? Some clues appear in the U.S.’s public data. The country has had measles cases every week since January 2025. That would be 20 months of weekly measles cases at this point. Of course, maybe genomic data points will save the day. Maybe they won’t. Regardless of the outcome of our meeting and PAHO’s decision in November, the U.S. clearly has a measles problem, as do Canada and Mexico. Elimination status marks whether a country has stopped sustained domestic transmission. Losing that status would signal a consequential reversal, evidence that the systems and protections that once kept measles at bay no longer do. We can and must do more than we’re doing to end the extraordinary spread of measles in our country and beyond. The nation needs strong, positive communications to the public about the importance of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccination and promotion of health care providers as trusted advisers on immunizations. A dedicated communication campaign led by the federal government would be usual in past years at this stage. These communications need clear, vocal, and regular support from the highest levels of the U.S. government. Initiatives to better understand and address vaccine hesitancy are also urgently needed. Advertisement Measles is a brutal disease that has no medical cure. Parents of children made sickest must wait it out in the hospital, despairingly wondering whether their child will die. That level of risk is indefensible in 2026 — more than 25 years after the United States achieved measles elimination. Kids are suffering and dying from a disease we already know how to prevent, and that failure is entirely ours. Noel Brewer is the Gillings distinguished professor in public health at the University of North Carolina. He chairs the U.S. committee that reviews the annual CDC measles reports to verify whether the U.S. maintains or loses measles elimination status. Letter to the editor Have an opinion on this essay? analysis.brief_en: This article discusses the U.S. National Verification Committee's assessment of the country's measles elimination status in 2026. The committee, which includes the author and colleagues, is reviewing data to determine if the U.S. has maintained its elimination status or is at risk of losing it. news.content: News Sports Life Business Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Measles cases surge across the country. Is Oklahoma affected? Isa Almeida The Oklahoman Aug. 6, 2026, 5:04 a.m. CT The number of measles cases confirmed so far this year in the United States has reached 2,318, more than all of 2025 and the highest in 35 years, according to the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In Oklahoma, however, only one case of measles was reported in 2026. The case was reported in Norman during the week of January 26. There has been no reported exposure recently. Southern neighbor Texas has reported 190 cases in 2026, and both Utah and South Carolina have reported over 500. Despite being declared officially eliminated from the United States in 2000, measles still affects some Americans every year. The viral disease, which affected hundreds of thousands before the vaccine was licensed in 1963, had claimed under 1,000 victims annually in the 21st century, with some years having under 100 cases. That hasn't been the case in the past two years, which have seen cases rising past the 2,000 mark. Still, measles rarely results in hospitalization or deaths. The disease being eliminated from the country means there is no measles spreading within the country and new cases are only found when someone contracts measles abroad and returns to the country, but recent outbreaks have increased the numbers. According to CDC data, nearly half of measles victims in 2026 have been between the age ranges of five and 19, with 93% being unvaccinated. In Oklahoma, only 88.7% of the population has received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. The CDC said that when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity, or herd immunity. The MMR vaccine is among the required immunizations to attend school in Oklahoma starting at kindergarten, though families can file for exemptions due to personal, religious or medical reasons. Here's what to know about measles, including symptoms and how to report it. What are measles symptoms? According to the Oklahoma State Department of Health, measles symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, watery eyes and a red blotchy rash starting on the face then spreading to the rest of the body. Symptoms are likely to appear as early as seven days after infection, but could be as late as 21 days. After three to five days, a red rash appears, beginning at the hairline and spreading down the rest of the body over the next few days. When the rash appears, a person’s fever may spike to more than 104 degrees, the OSDH said. Measles could affect all groups, but are particularly concerning among children under five, pregnant women, adults older than 20 years old and those with compromised immune systems. Common complications are ear infections and diarrhea. Serious complications include pneumonia, encephalitis (swelling of the brain) and in some cases, death. How is measles spread? Is measles contagious? Measles is highly contagious. According to the CDC, if one person contracts the disease up to 90% of unprotected people close to them will become infected. The virus can be passed from person to person by airborne droplets from coughing and sneezing, by contact with nose and throat secretions from ill persons or by touching a contaminated surface. Infected individuals can be contagious four days before their rash starts and through four days after the rash appears. The measles virus can live up to two hours in the air after an infected person leaves an area. If infected, the sick person must work with the health department to determine when it is safe to return to work, school, daycare or other public settings. How to prevent measles The best way to prevent measles is through the MMR vaccine, a combination of measles, mumps and rubella. The vaccine works with two doses, one recommended for all children at 12 to 15 months of age and again at four to six years of age. If someone has not received the second dose by age six, it can be taken at any point thereafter. The two doses commonly provide lifelong immunity. How to report measles in Oklahoma All Oklahoma health care providers and laboratories are mandated to report cases of disease and conditions to the OSDH, per Title 63 Oklahoma Statute (O.S.) 1981 §1-503 Measles is typically diagnosed through a combination of physical signs, health history and laboratory tests, including identifying fever with a spreading rash, throat swabs and blood tests. What vaccines are required to attend Oklahoma schools? These requirements apply to both public and private institutions, though private schools could set stricter rules or choose not to accept state-allowed exemptions. Child care (birth to three years) Four doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) One to four doses of PCV (pneumococcal) One to four doses of Hib (Haemophilus influenza type B) One dose of varicella Three doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza Preschool (four years) Four doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) One dose of varicella Three doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza, second varicella dose at four years old, IPV on or after fourth birthday Kindergarten to sixth grade Five doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) Two doses of MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) One dose of varicella Four doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza, second varicella dose at four years old, IPV on or after fourth birthday Seventh to 12th grade One dose of Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis) Five doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) Two doses of MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) One dose of varicella Four doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza, two to three doses of HPV (human papillomavirus), one to two doses of MCV4 (meningococcal ACWY), two to three doses of Men B (meningitis group B) Post-secondary institutions These apply to all new or incoming students attending public or private post-secondary institutions in Oklahoma. Non-medical exemptions can be provided. Hepatitis B MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) Meningococcal (for students living on-campus) Who is exempt from required vaccinations in Oklahoma? In Oklahoma, there are several ways to claim an exemption from the required vaccines. Children with specific medical contraindications to any or all immunizations may be allowed to attend if the medical reason is stated and this statement is signed by a licensed physician and submitted to the school, child care facility or Head Start, according to the Oklahoma State Department of Health. Children whose parents object to immunizations based on religious teachings or personal beliefs may also seek an exemption. Isa Almeida is a trending reporter for The Oklahoman. news.content_original: News Sports Life Business Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Measles cases surge across the country. Is Oklahoma affected? Isa Almeida The Oklahoman Aug. 6, 2026, 5:04 a.m. CT The number of measles cases confirmed so far this year in the United States has reached 2,318, more than all of 2025 and the highest in 35 years, according to the latest data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In Oklahoma, however, only one case of measles was reported in 2026. The case was reported in Norman during the week of January 26. There has been no reported exposure recently. Southern neighbor Texas has reported 190 cases in 2026, and both Utah and South Carolina have reported over 500. Despite being declared officially eliminated from the United States in 2000, measles still affects some Americans every year. The viral disease, which affected hundreds of thousands before the vaccine was licensed in 1963, had claimed under 1,000 victims annually in the 21st century, with some years having under 100 cases. That hasn't been the case in the past two years, which have seen cases rising past the 2,000 mark. Still, measles rarely results in hospitalization or deaths. The disease being eliminated from the country means there is no measles spreading within the country and new cases are only found when someone contracts measles abroad and returns to the country, but recent outbreaks have increased the numbers. According to CDC data, nearly half of measles victims in 2026 have been between the age ranges of five and 19, with 93% being unvaccinated. In Oklahoma, only 88.7% of the population has received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. The CDC said that when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity, or herd immunity. The MMR vaccine is among the required immunizations to attend school in Oklahoma starting at kindergarten, though families can file for exemptions due to personal, religious or medical reasons. Here's what to know about measles, including symptoms and how to report it. What are measles symptoms? According to the Oklahoma State Department of Health, measles symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, watery eyes and a red blotchy rash starting on the face then spreading to the rest of the body. Symptoms are likely to appear as early as seven days after infection, but could be as late as 21 days. After three to five days, a red rash appears, beginning at the hairline and spreading down the rest of the body over the next few days. When the rash appears, a person’s fever may spike to more than 104 degrees, the OSDH said. Measles could affect all groups, but are particularly concerning among children under five, pregnant women, adults older than 20 years old and those with compromised immune systems. Common complications are ear infections and diarrhea. Serious complications include pneumonia, encephalitis (swelling of the brain) and in some cases, death. How is measles spread? Is measles contagious? Measles is highly contagious. According to the CDC, if one person contracts the disease up to 90% of unprotected people close to them will become infected. The virus can be passed from person to person by airborne droplets from coughing and sneezing, by contact with nose and throat secretions from ill persons or by touching a contaminated surface. Infected individuals can be contagious four days before their rash starts and through four days after the rash appears. The measles virus can live up to two hours in the air after an infected person leaves an area. If infected, the sick person must work with the health department to determine when it is safe to return to work, school, daycare or other public settings. How to prevent measles The best way to prevent measles is through the MMR vaccine, a combination of measles, mumps and rubella. The vaccine works with two doses, one recommended for all children at 12 to 15 months of age and again at four to six years of age. If someone has not received the second dose by age six, it can be taken at any point thereafter. The two doses commonly provide lifelong immunity. How to report measles in Oklahoma All Oklahoma health care providers and laboratories are mandated to report cases of disease and conditions to the OSDH, per Title 63 Oklahoma Statute (O.S.) 1981 §1-503 Measles is typically diagnosed through a combination of physical signs, health history and laboratory tests, including identifying fever with a spreading rash, throat swabs and blood tests. What vaccines are required to attend Oklahoma schools? These requirements apply to both public and private institutions, though private schools could set stricter rules or choose not to accept state-allowed exemptions. Child care (birth to three years) Four doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) One to four doses of PCV (pneumococcal) One to four doses of Hib (Haemophilus influenza type B) One dose of varicella Three doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza Preschool (four years) Four doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) One dose of varicella Three doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza, second varicella dose at four years old, IPV on or after fourth birthday Kindergarten to sixth grade Five doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) Two doses of MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) One dose of varicella Four doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza, second varicella dose at four years old, IPV on or after fourth birthday Seventh to 12th grade One dose of Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis) Five doses of DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis) Two doses of MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) One dose of varicella Four doses of IPV (polio) Two doses of Hep A (hepatitis A) Three doses of Hep B (hepatitis B) Recommended: seasonal influenza, two to three doses of HPV (human papillomavirus), one to two doses of MCV4 (meningococcal ACWY), two to three doses of Men B (meningitis group B) Post-secondary institutions These apply to all new or incoming students attending public or private post-secondary institutions in Oklahoma. Non-medical exemptions can be provided. Hepatitis B MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) Meningococcal (for students living on-campus) Who is exempt from required vaccinations in Oklahoma? In Oklahoma, there are several ways to claim an exemption from the required vaccines. Children with specific medical contraindications to any or all immunizations may be allowed to attend if the medical reason is stated and this statement is signed by a licensed physician and submitted to the school, child care facility or Head Start, according to the Oklahoma State Department of Health. Children whose parents object to immunizations based on religious teachings or personal beliefs may also seek an exemption. Isa Almeida is a trending reporter for The Oklahoman. Have a story idea for Isa? She can be reached at ialmeida@oklahoman.com or on X/Twitter at @ialmeidasports. Got it Edition CA NY US News Metro Long Island Politics World News Search Search Recommended Skip to main content Metro Measles panic at popular SoCal theme park after infected guest roamed for hours By Daniel Farr Published Aug. 6, 2026, 12:41 a.m. ET 154154 Comments See more of our coverage in your search results. Add The California Post on Google A trip to Universal Studios Hollywood came with a frightening plot twist after a measles-infected guest spent 11 hours inside the packed park, sparking a public health alert. Health officials warned Wednesday that anyone who visited the Southern California attraction on Sunday between 10 a.m. and 9 p.m. may have been exposed to the highly contagious virus. 10 A computer illustration shows a measles virus particle. Getty Images/Science Photo Libra 10 The Universal globe is seen outside Universal Studios Hollywood. Bloomberg via Getty Images The alert comes as measles continues its dramatic resurgence across the US. The country has recorded 2,371 confirmed cases in 2026 as of late July, the highest annual total since 1991, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “With summer travel underway, the risk of exposure to infectious diseases may increase,” Muntu Davis, county public health officer wrote. “We urge everyone to confirm their immunity and get the MMR vaccine if needed, especially before traveling and attending crowded events.” Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes. news.content_title: Ventura County reports first measles case in nine years
news.content: News Sports Opinion Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Ventura County reports first measles case in nine years Tom Kisken Ventura County Star Aug. 5, 2026, 4:48 p.m. PT Ventura County's first measles cases in nine years was announced Aug. 5. Sites where other people could have been exposed include Universal Studios Hollywood. A Ventura County resident has tested positive for measles in the county’s first such case in nine years, public health officials said. Dr. Uldine Castel, county health officer, said the case is linked to international travel. She said it's possible other people could have been exposed to the highly contagious illness at several sites ranging from an Oxnard movie theater to a Ventura medical office. Los Angeles County officials said an infected person also visited Universal Studios Hollywood on July 26. Castel confirmed it was the same case. The disease was confirmed late in the afternoon on Aug. 4. Castel offered little information about the infected person but said the individual is an adult who had returned home from a trip to another country and was isolating at home. Health officials were working at identifying people who were in physical contact with the infected person and may have been exposed, Castel said. “We have found a few contacts, and they’ve all been actively engaged with our communicable disease staff,” she said, noting that in some cases blood has been drawn to confirm a person has been infected and is immune. She also expressed confidence in efforts to control further transmission. "Our team has mobilized quickly to help alert the community and try to contain the spread," she said in a news release. "Ventura County is well positioned to respond effectively with our experienced staff and strong vaccination rates among our residents." Health officials said people could possibly have been exposed at the following times and locations: July 26, about 8 a.m. to 10 a.m.: Subway restaurant, 1941 N. Rose Ave., Suite 600, Oxnard July 26, 10 a.m. to 9 p.m.: Universal Studios Hollywood, Universal City July 27 to Aug. 1: Hacienda Furniture and Mattress, 3200 S. Saviers Road, Oxnard July 31, about 7:30 p.m. to midnight.: Cinemark Century Riverpark theater, 2766 Seaglass Way, Oxnard Aug. 1, about 9:30 a.m. to 11 a.m.: Walgreens, 1801 N. Rose Ave., Oxnard Aug. 2, about 9 a.m. to 11 a.m.: Kaiser Permanente medical office, 4949 Market St., Ventura Officials said other locations of possible exposures were being investigated. They said people who may have been exposed should contact their doctors and check their vaccination status. Children should receive their first vaccine dose between 12 months and 15 months of age. The second dose should come when they are 4 years to 6 years old. Adults who may have been exposed and don't know if they've been vaccinated should reach out to their physicians. People who may have been exposed are at higher risk if they are: pregnant, an infant younger than 12 months old, a person with weakened immunities or someone who is unvaccinated. Symptoms of measles usually appear one or two weeks after exposure and can last up to 10 days. They include a high fever, cough, runny nose and red watery eyes. A rash typically appears three to five days after the first symptoms, starting at the hairline and spreading downward across the body. Public health officials said people who develop symptoms should call a health care provider immediately but should not visit a medical facility without notification. People with symptoms should isolate and stay away from work, school or other public places. Ventura County’s last reported measles cases came in 2017 when three county residents and two other non-residents staying in the county tested positive for the illness. Two years earlier, when an outbreak linked to Disneyland spread across California and other states, 14 measles cases were reported in the county. This year has brought a surge of measles cases in the United States. Castel said the local case is not linked to other domestic outbreaks because it was triggered by international travel. Castel said the county’s high measles vaccination rate and the quick response of health workers are good signs. “I feel really confident,” she said. "We have an incredible staff that knows how to do this." People with questions can call the county’s measles information line at 805-652-7599. Doctors can report suspected cases by calling 805-981-5201. Tom Kisken covers health care and other news for the Ventura County Star. Reach him at tom.kisken@vcstar.com. news.content: Englishहिन्दी Videos Photos Yoga Asanas Herbs Parenting Baby Names Useful Links Advertise With Us Disclaimer Terms & Conditions Privacy Policy Contact Us Author Profiles Archives Complaint Follow THS Latest News Diseases Type 1 Diabetes Type 2 Diabetes Cancer Heart Attack Pneumonia Diseases A-Z Diet & Fitness Pregnancy Conceiving Infertility Labour & Delivery Breastfeeding Baby Names Beauty AYUSH Herbs Unani Siddha Homeopathy Naturopathy Home Remedies Organ Donation Webstories Logout Health News Diseases Conditions Study finds single US measles outbreak can cost millions: How to protect yourself Study finds single US measles outbreak can cost millions: How to protect yourself A new study led by the New Mexico Department of Health reveals a single measles outbreak in the US can cost millions. Learn practical prevention tips and why vaccination remains the strongest defense. Written By: N. Lothungbeni Humtsoe | Published : August 5, 2026 10:15 AM IST Share Share Article ✕ Copied Measles in US. Measles is a highly contagious illness that spreads from person to person through the air and via respiratory droplets. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) about 95,000 people died in connection with the illness in 2024. Although vaccination has decreased the death rate of measles from 750,000 in 2000 to 95,000 in 2025, scientists state that a single measles outbreak in the country can cost billions of dollars. A study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine indicates that nearly $5.4 million was invested in preventing the US measles outbreak in 2025. This figure includes expenses for medical care and public health services for vaccination-related activities of patients affected by the contagious illness. The outbreak resulted in quarantine, emergency vaccination campaigns, hospitalisations and widespread public health measures beyond the 100 confirmed cases indicating the actual burden of measles is far greater than the patient. Researchers say each case of measles triggers a chain reaction, affecting families, health care providers and public health systems. With declining vaccination rates in the United States, experts say taking measures to prevent outbreaks is much cheaper and more effective than once the virus spreads. The deaths of at least seven Indigenous children have exposed how gaps in immunisation, surveillance, emergency referral systems, and culturally responsive healthcare continue to leave some of Bangladesh’s most isolated communities dangerously vulnerable Sumit Banik 04 August, 2026, 06:15 pm Last modified: 04 August, 2026, 06:28 pm Photo Caption: Khumi parents care for their child in the isolation ward at Ruma Upazila Health Complex amid a measles outbreak that has killed seven children in Bandarban's remote Ruma upazila. Photo: TBS The recent measles outbreak in Ruma Upazila of Bangladesh's Bandarban Hill District has exposed a painful reality: for some children, where they are born can determine whether they live or die. Since early June, dozens of children from remote Indigenous communities have fallen ill with measles. According to media reports, "Seven Khumi children die as Measles outbreak strikes Bandarban's Ruma" ultimately at least seven children have died, while many others have required medical treatment. Behind these heartbreaking statistics lies a deeper public health story—one that extends far beyond a single infectious disease outbreak. Measles is not a mysterious or untreatable disease. It is one of the world's most contagious viral infections, yet it is also one of the most preventable through routine immunisation. When children die from measles today, the tragedy rarely reflects the virus alone. More often, it reveals gaps in immunisation coverage, delayed care-seeking, weak disease surveillance, inadequate referral systems, and persistent inequities in access to healthcare. The situation in Ruma illustrates exactly this reality. Many of the affected children belong to the Mro and Khumi Indigenous communities living in some of Bangladesh's most geographically isolated areas. Their villages are scattered across steep hills, dense forests, and locations that often require hours of walking before reaching the nearest road. During the monsoon season, travel becomes even more difficult as heavy rains, landslides, and swollen streams further isolate communities. Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel Geography, however, is only part of the challenge. Health-seeking behaviour in many Indigenous communities has evolved over generations within unique cultural, social, and spiritual traditions. Families may initially seek advice from community elders or traditional healers before considering formal healthcare. Language barriers, financial hardship, limited health literacy, and previous experiences with inaccessible services may further delay treatment. These realities should never be interpreted as resistance to modern medicine. Rather, they highlight the importance of designing health systems that are culturally responsive, respectful, and trusted by the communities they serve. From an epidemiological perspective, the outbreak demonstrates how infectious diseases exploit health system vulnerabilities. Measles spreads rapidly wherever immunity gaps exist. A single infected child can transmit the virus to many susceptible children, particularly in communities with low vaccination coverage. Once transmission begins in remote areas where early detection is difficult and referral pathways are weak, controlling the outbreak becomes significantly more challenging. This is why outbreak preparedness cannot begin after children start dying. Public health systems must identify vulnerable populations before outbreaks occur. Regular vaccination coverage assessments, active surveillance, rapid response teams, and community engagement should become routine components of healthcare delivery in hard-to-reach areas rather than emergency measures implemented only after a crisis emerges. The Ruma outbreak also reminds us that equity is one of the strongest determinants of health. Although Bangladesh has achieved remarkable success in childhood immunisation over the past decades, national averages can conceal local disparities. A country may report high vaccination coverage while small pockets of under-immunised populations remain vulnerable. These "zero-dose" or under-vaccinated communities often become the epicentre of outbreaks. Reaching the last child is invariably the most difficult—but it is also the most important. A comprehensive response requires more than emergency vaccination campaigns. First, immunisation services must be redesigned for difficult terrain. Instead of expecting families to travel long distances to health facilities, outreach vaccination teams should routinely visit remote villages with reliable cold-chain support and adequate staffing. Second, community-based surveillance should be strengthened. Local volunteers, teachers, religious leaders, and trained community health workers can help identify suspected cases early and notify health authorities before widespread transmission occurs. Third, emergency referral systems require urgent investment. In many parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, reaching a hospital can take several hours or even an entire day. Dedicated ambulances suitable for mountainous terrain, community transport mechanisms, emergency communication networks, and referral coordination can significantly reduce delays in life-saving treatment. Fourth, culturally appropriate risk communication is essential. Health education materials should be available in local languages and developed in partnership with Indigenous leaders, ensuring that vaccination campaigns are built on trust rather than assumptions. Communities are far more likely to participate when health interventions acknowledge their culture and involve respected local voices. Fifth, the health workforce serving remote hill districts deserves greater investment. Recruiting and retaining trained healthcare professionals in geographically isolated regions remains a persistent challenge. Incentive packages, continuous professional support, telemedicine consultations, and training local community members as frontline health workers can help bridge this gap. The lessons extend beyond Bandarban. Climate change, extreme weather events, and difficult terrain will continue to complicate healthcare delivery in many remote parts of Bangladesh. Future outbreaks—whether measles, dengue, cholera, or emerging infectious diseases—will disproportionately affect communities that remain underserved by the health system. Strengthening resilience in these areas should therefore be viewed not merely as a humanitarian obligation but as a national public health priority. Ultimately, this outbreak is not simply about measles. It is about whether every child in Bangladesh enjoys an equal opportunity to survive, regardless of ethnicity, geography, or socioeconomic status. It is about whether health equity remains an aspiration or becomes an operational principle guiding public policy. The deaths of these children should not be remembered only as another headline from a remote hill district. They should become a turning point for strengthening inclusive healthcare, improving outbreak preparedness, and ensuring that no child dies from a vaccine-preventable disease simply because healthcare arrives too late. Distance should never determine survival. Every child deserves timely vaccination, prompt diagnosis, quality treatment, and an equal chance at life. The measles outbreak in Ruma is a painful reminder of how far we still have to go—but it also offers a clear roadmap for building a stronger, more equitable, and more resilient public health system for all Bangladeshis. The deaths of at least seven Indigenous children have exposed how gaps in immunisation, surveillance, emergency referral systems, and culturally responsive healthcare continue to leave some of Bangladesh’s most isolated communities dangerously vulnerable Sumit Banik 04 August, 2026, 06:15 pm Last modified: 04 August, 2026, 06:28 pm Photo Caption: Khumi parents care for their child in the isolation ward at Ruma Upazila Health Complex amid a measles outbreak that has killed seven children in Bandarban's remote Ruma upazila. Photo: TBS The recent measles outbreak in Ruma Upazila of Bangladesh's Bandarban Hill District has exposed a painful reality: for some children, where they are born can determine whether they live or die. Since early June, dozens of children from remote Indigenous communities have fallen ill with measles. According to media reports, "Seven Khumi children die as Measles outbreak strikes Bandarban's Ruma" ultimately at least seven children have died, while many others have required medical treatment. Behind these heartbreaking statistics lies a deeper public health story—one that extends far beyond a single infectious disease outbreak. Measles is not a mysterious or untreatable disease. It is one of the world's most contagious viral infections, yet it is also one of the most preventable through routine immunisation. When children die from measles today, the tragedy rarely reflects the virus alone. More often, it reveals gaps in immunisation coverage, delayed care-seeking, weak disease surveillance, inadequate referral systems, and persistent inequities in access to healthcare. The situation in Ruma illustrates exactly this reality. Many of the affected children belong to the Mro and Khumi Indigenous communities living in some of Bangladesh's most geographically isolated areas. Their villages are scattered across steep hills, dense forests, and locations that often require hours of walking before reaching the nearest road. During the monsoon season, travel becomes even more difficult as heavy rains, landslides, and swollen streams further isolate communities. Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel Geography, however, is only part of the challenge. Health-seeking behaviour in many Indigenous communities has evolved over generations within unique cultural, social, and spiritual traditions. Families may initially seek advice from community elders or traditional healers before considering formal healthcare. Language barriers, financial hardship, limited health literacy, and previous experiences with inaccessible services may further delay treatment. These realities should never be interpreted as resistance to modern medicine. Rather, they highlight the importance of designing health systems that are culturally responsive, respectful, and trusted by the communities they serve. From an epidemiological perspective, the outbreak demonstrates how infectious diseases exploit health system vulnerabilities. Measles spreads rapidly wherever immunity gaps exist. A single infected child can transmit the virus to many susceptible children, particularly in communities with low vaccination coverage. Once transmission begins in remote areas where early detection is difficult and referral pathways are weak, controlling the outbreak becomes significantly more challenging. This is why outbreak preparedness cannot begin after children start dying. Public health systems must identify vulnerable populations before outbreaks occur. Regular vaccination coverage assessments, active surveillance, rapid response teams, and community engagement should become routine components of healthcare delivery in hard-to-reach areas rather than emergency measures implemented only after a crisis emerges. The Ruma outbreak also reminds us that equity is one of the strongest determinants of health. Although Bangladesh has achieved remarkable success in childhood immunisation over the past decades, national averages can conceal local disparities. A country may report high vaccination coverage while small pockets of under-immunised populations remain vulnerable. These "zero-dose" or under-vaccinated communities often become the epicentre of outbreaks. Reaching the last child is invariably the most difficult—but it is also the most important. A comprehensive response requires more than emergency vaccination campaigns. First, immunisation services must be redesigned for difficult terrain. Instead of expecting families to travel long distances to health facilities, outreach vaccination teams should routinely visit remote villages with reliable cold-chain support and adequate staffing. Second, community-based surveillance should be strengthened. Local volunteers, teachers, religious leaders, and trained community health workers can help identify suspected cases early and notify health authorities before widespread transmission occurs. Third, emergency referral systems require urgent investment. In many parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, reaching a hospital can take several hours or even an entire day. Dedicated ambulances suitable for mountainous terrain, community transport mechanisms, emergency communication networks, and referral coordination can significantly reduce delays in life-saving treatment. Fourth, culturally appropriate risk communication is essential. Health education materials should be available in local languages and developed in partnership with Indigenous leaders, ensuring that vaccination campaigns are built on trust rather than assumptions. Communities are far more likely to participate when health interventions acknowledge their culture and involve respected local voices. Fifth, the health workforce serving remote hill districts deserves greater investment. Recruiting and retaining trained healthcare professionals in geographically isolated regions remains a persistent challenge. Incentive packages, continuous professional support, telemedicine consultations, and training local community members as frontline health workers can help bridge this gap. The lessons extend beyond Bandarban. Climate change, extreme weather events, and difficult terrain will continue to complicate healthcare delivery in many remote parts of Bangladesh. Future outbreaks—whether measles, dengue, cholera, or emerging infectious diseases—will disproportionately affect communities that remain underserved by the health system. Strengthening resilience in these areas should therefore be viewed not merely as a humanitarian obligation but as a national public health priority. Ultimately, this outbreak is not simply about measles. It is about whether every child in Bangladesh enjoys an equal opportunity to survive, regardless of ethnicity, geography, or socioeconomic status. It is about whether health equity remains an aspiration or becomes an operational principle guiding public policy. The deaths of these children should not be remembered only as another headline from a remote hill district. They should become a turning point for strengthening inclusive healthcare, improving outbreak preparedness, and ensuring that no child dies from a vaccine-preventable disease simply because healthcare arrives too late. Distance should never determine survival. Every child deserves timely vaccination, prompt diagnosis, quality treatment, and an equal chance at life. The measles outbreak in Ruma is a painful reminder of how far we still have to go—but it also offers a clear roadmap for building a stronger, more equitable, and more resilient public health system for all Bangladeshis. Sumit Banik is a Public Health Activist and Trainer. analysis.brief_en: A measles outbreak in Ruma Upazila, Bandarban Hill District, Bangladesh, has killed at least seven Indigenous children since early June, with dozens more hospitalized. The tragedy exposes deep systemic gaps: low routine immunization coverage, delayed care-seeking rooted in cultural and geographic barriers, weak disease surveillance, and inadequate emergency referral pathways in remote hill and forest communities. Monsoon rains and landslides further isolate villages, delaying access to care and enabling rapid spread among unvaccinated children. Experts emphasize that the crisis reflects broader inequities in health access rather than vaccine failure alone, urging culturally responsive outreach vaccination, community-based surveillance, terrain-appropriate ambulances, and investment in the local health workforce to prevent future outbreaks.

Advertisement Updated: 4:24 PM EDT Aug 4, 2026 Editorial Standards i Julian Nazario Digital Content Producer Maryland confirms 13th measles case after possible exposure at Elkton hospital Updated: 4:24 PM EDT Aug 4, 2026 Editorial Standards i Julian Nazario Digital Content Producer The Maryland Department of Health said it had confirmed a case of measles in a Maryland resident after a possible exposure in the Upper Eastern Shore region. The new case is the 13th confirmed case in the state this year. Advertisement According to MDH, anyone who visited ChristianaCare Union Hospital Emergency Department in Elkton on Aug. 2 from 7 p.m. to 10:15 p.m. may have been exposed to the infection. Last week, the department had warned of a possible exposure at the same emergency room on July 30, warning those who visited the department from 3:00 a.m. - 7:15 a.m. It can take up to three weeks for symptoms to appear. Think you may have been exposed? Here's what to do Were you vaccinated for measles? If you have received two doses of a measles-containing vaccine, or were born before 1957, you are generally considered protected. Check your immunization status securely online via My Immunization Record (MyIR). MDH recommends all eligible people get fully vaccinated against measles. The measles vaccine is routinely recommended at 12-15 months of age for the first dose and the second dose at 4-6 years old. Sometimes a dose is given as early as six to 12 months if there is travel planned to an area that has ongoing measles transmission. Monitor for early symptoms : People, especially those not fully vaccinated or otherwise immune to measles, who were at any of these locations during the possible exposure times should monitor themselves for any early symptoms of measles for 21 days after the potential exposure. Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Video above: Doctor shares tips amid confirmed measles case in Maryland Not fully vaccinated or otherwise immune? If you are not fully vaccinated or otherwise immune to measles (i.e., you already had measles) and you might have been exposed, call your health care provider or your local health department to discuss the best next steps for you. If your exposure occurred on or after April 14, 2026, you may qualify for post-exposure treatments. What are the symptoms of measles? Early symptoms of measles are a fever of more than 101 degrees Fahrenheit; runny nose; cough; and red, watery eyes. Usually, one to four days after the early symptoms, a red rash appears on the face and spreads to the rest of the body. Symptoms typically develop 10 to 14 days after exposure but can develop as soon as seven days and as long as 21 days after exposure. A person with measles is contagious, beginning four days before the rash appears until four days after the rash begins. Call your health care provider : Exposed individuals who develop a fever or other symptoms of measles should not go to child care, school, work, or out in public, and should contact their health care provider. They should call their health care provider before going to a waiting room or emergency department so that the facility can take measures to prevent measles from spreading to others. Is measles contagious? Health officials describe measles as a highly contagious disease that is spread easily through the air when an infectious person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area. The disease is also spread by direct contact and after touching infected surfaces.
