Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Portland Clackamas Kaiser Clinic Becomes Latest Measles Site as Oregon Cases Climb By Samuel Hansen Published on August 07, 2026 Source: Google Street View People who visited the Kaiser Permanente Mt. Scott Medical Office in Clackamas last Thursday afternoon may have been exposed to measles, according to the Oregon Health Authority. The agency says anyone at the clinic between 1:35 p.m. and 3:44 p.m. last Thursday could have encountered the virus, making it the latest site in a string of Portland-area exposure alerts this year. The clinic sits at 9800 Southeast Sunnyside Road in Clackamas County, according to KGW, which reported that state and county health officials identified the site after an infected patient spent more than two hours there. As The Oregonian/OregonLive reports, the Oregon Health Authority has flagged this Kaiser Permanente location as the latest confirmed exposure point in the Portland metro area, with other recent risk areas including Clark County, Beaverton, Gresham and parts of Portland itself. Measles spreads through coughs and sneezes, and the virus can remain infectious in the air of an enclosed space for up to two hours after an infected person leaves, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Symptoms typically appear seven to 21 days after exposure and can include fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, per the same account, sometimes followed by a rash of flat red spots that begins on the face and spreads across the body. Oregon Health Authority guidelines note that infected individuals become contagious four days before the rash appears and remain contagious for four days after it shows up, which helps explain how the virus can spread in a waiting room before anyone realizes they are sick. A Pattern Stretching Back to January This is not the first time a Kaiser Permanente facility in Clackamas County has landed on the exposure list this year. Clackamas County confirmed its first measles case of 2026 in mid-January, which triggered a potential exposure alert at the Kaiser Permanente Sunnyside Medical Center emergency department on January 26, according to Oregon Public Broadcasting. Health officials at the time noted that most confirmed local cases involved unvaccinated residents without international travel history. Less than a month before Thursday's alert, three Providence Health facilities — Providence Immediate Care in Happy Valley, Providence Willamette Falls Medical Center in Oregon City, and Providence Portland Medical Center — were flagged as exposure sites between July 9 and July 12, Oregon Public Broadcasting reported. Urgent care centers and emergency departments have repeatedly become exposure points this year when infected patients arrive without calling ahead, a pattern Hoodline has tracked through incidents from a midnight ER scare in Oregon City to a Beaverton trampoline park scare last month. Why Oregon Keeps Seeing New Exposure Sites The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 2,465 confirmed measles cases across 47 U.S. jurisdictions as of Thursday, making 2026 the worst year for measles nationally in more than three decades since the disease was declared eliminated in the country in 2000. The Oregonian/OregonLive reports that Oregon itself has recorded 40 measles cases this year, according to CDC figures. Falling vaccination rates help explain why the Portland area keeps generating new exposure sites. The Oregon Health Authority reported in May that nonmedical vaccine exemptions among Oregon kindergarteners hit a record 10.9% for the 2025–2026 school year, up from 6.9% just a few years earlier, with exemptions for the second MMR dose reaching 9.4%. Separately, state immunization data showed only 85.6% of Oregon kindergarteners were up to date on required vaccines that same year, leaving more than a third of the state's K-12 schools below the 93% threshold that epidemiologists say is needed for herd immunity, according to The Lund Report. To catch spread that clinical testing might miss, the Oregon Health Authority launched a statewide wastewater surveillance dashboard in February that tracks measles virus concentrations in sewage across the state's counties, since infected people shed the virus whether or not they seek medical care. Hoodline previously covered the launch of that quiet wastewater alarm system. What To Do If You Were Exposed Measles has been largely non-fatal in countries where the vaccine is available, but it can be more dangerous for children, older adults and immunocompromised people, per The Oregonian/OregonLive. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles, and the Oregon Health Authority recommends vaccination to lower infection risk. The CDC notes that susceptible people exposed to measles can still receive an MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure to prevent or lessen illness, or immune globulin within six days for high-risk patients such as infants, pregnant women or immunocompromised individuals. The Oregon Health Authority is urging anyone experiencing measles symptoms, including a rash or runny nose, to call ahead before visiting a medical facility rather than walking into a waiting room. Calling ahead helps prevent exposing other patients who may not be immune, health officials say, a message that has repeated through nearly every exposure alert issued across the Portland metro area this year. The Oregon Health Authority reported in May that nonmedical vaccine exemptions among Oregon kindergarteners hit a record 10.9% for the 2025–2026 school year, up from 6.9% just a few years earlier, with exemptions for the second MMR dose reaching 9.4%. Separately, state immunization data showed only 85.6% of Oregon kindergarteners were up to date on required vaccines that same year, leaving more than a third of the state's K-12 schools below the 93% threshold that epidemiologists say is needed for herd immunity, according to The Lund Report. To catch spread that clinical testing might miss, the Oregon Health Authority launched a statewide wastewater surveillance dashboard in February that tracks measles virus concentrations in sewage across the state's counties, since infected people shed the virus whether or not they seek medical care. Hoodline previously covered the launch of that quiet wastewater alarm system. What To Do If You Were Exposed Measles has been largely non-fatal in countries where the vaccine is available, but it can be more dangerous for children, older adults and immunocompromised people, per The Oregonian/OregonLive. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles, and the Oregon Health Authority recommends vaccination to lower infection risk. The CDC notes that susceptible people exposed to measles can still receive an MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure to prevent or lessen illness, or immune globulin within six days for high-risk patients such as infants, pregnant women or immunocompromised individuals. The Oregon Health Authority is urging anyone experiencing measles symptoms, including a rash or runny nose, to call ahead before visiting a medical facility rather than walking into a waiting room. Calling ahead helps prevent exposing other patients who may not be immune, health officials say, a message that has repeated through nearly every exposure alert issued across the Portland metro area this year. By Elizabeth Chavolla • Published August 5, 2026 • Updated on August 5, 2026 at 2:26 pm Log in or create a free profile to save articles BOOKMARKER 0:00 Play 0:00 / 1:14 Unmute ShareToggle Fullscreen NBC Universal, Inc. Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease caused by a virus that can lead to severe complications and death. Ventura County health officials confirmed Wednesday a case of measles linked to international travel, marking the county's first reported case since 2017. The Ventura County Public Health Department said that it is conducting an investigation and working closely with health care providers and people who may have been exposed to help prevent further spread of the virus. Stream Los Angeles News for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE "Our team mobilized quickly to alert the community and try to contain the spread," Ventura County Public Health Officer Dr. Uldine Castel said in a statement. The virus can remain in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Health officials said people who are unvaccinated or have not completed the recommended vaccination series face a higher risk of infection. Those who are fully vaccinated or were born before 1957 have an extremely low risk of contracting the disease. 3:11 New measles cases reported in Southern California A new measles case was reported in Southern California. Tracey Leong reports for the NBC4 News at 11 p.m. on Jan. 31, 2026. "Ventura County is well-prepared to respond effectively thanks to our experienced staff and the high vaccination rates among our residents," Castel said. The health department said people who were at the following locations during the listed dates and times may have been exposed to the virus: July 26: Subway, 1941 N. Rose Ave., Suite 600, Oxnard, from approximately 8:30 a.m. to 10 a.m. July 27 through Aug. 1: Hacienda Furniture and Mattress, 3200 S. Saviers Road, Oxnard. July 31: Cinemark Century Riverpark, 2766 Seaglass Way, Oxnard, from approximately 7:30 p.m. to midnight. Aug. 1: Walgreens, 1801 N. Rose Ave., Oxnard, from approximately 9:30 a.m. to 11 a.m. Aug. 2: Kaiser Permanente, 4949 Market St., Ventura, from approximately 9 a.m. to 11 a.m. For more information, residents can call Ventura County Public Health at (805) 652-7599 or visit the Ventura County Public Health website. Residents with potential exposure are advised to contact health authorities for guidance.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, August 7, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health New Mexico measles outbreak costs estimated at $5.4 million, including vaccination efforts by Bioengineer August 3, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A measles outbreak in New Mexico in 2025 generated an estimated $5.4 million in societal costs, according to a new analysis published in Annals of Internal Medicine. The estimate includes the resources used to investigate and contain the outbreak, medical care for infected people, and productivity losses among patients, families, contacts, and public health workers. Averaged across the 100 confirmed cases, the cost exceeded $53,000 per case, illustrating how quickly the economic consequences of a vaccine-preventable viral disease can extend beyond hospitals and clinics. The outbreak included one death and involved a substantial network of people who required monitoring or intervention. Researchers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases and the New Mexico Department of Health examined the response involving 100 confirmed patients, 205 exposed contacts, and 133 public health responders. Their analysis used a societal perspective, a standard economic framework that attempts to capture costs borne by health systems, government agencies, individuals, employers, and the wider community rather than focusing only on direct medical expenses. Discover more healthcare infections vaccine Health Measles is caused by measles virus, a highly contagious respiratory pathogen that spreads when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. The virus can remain suspended in the air for a period of time, allowing transmission even after an infected person has left an enclosed space. Once a case is identified, health officials must move rapidly to determine where transmission may have occurred, identify susceptible people, assess vaccination histories, and monitor exposed individuals during the incubation period. Those activities can consume considerable personnel time even when they prevent additional cases. The analysis estimated that public health activities accounted for approximately $3.2 million of the outbreak’s total cost. Vaccination-related work represented about $2.1 million of that amount, making it the largest individual component of the public health response. These efforts can include locating and reviewing immunization records, organizing vaccination clinics, administering doses, communicating with affected communities, and providing post-exposure vaccination when appropriate. Although such measures require immediate investment, they are intended to interrupt transmission before more people become infected. Containing measles also requires a detailed case-investigation infrastructure. Public health teams must verify diagnoses, collect and interpret laboratory information, reconstruct patients’ movements, notify people who may have been exposed, and coordinate with schools, health-care facilities, workplaces, and community organizations. Officials may need to recommend exclusion from group settings for people who are infected or who lack evidence of immunity. Each additional case can therefore create a new chain of investigations and notifications, multiplying the workload even when the number of patients remains relatively small. The researchers also included medical costs and productivity losses in their estimate. Medical expenses can arise from outpatient visits, diagnostic testing, emergency care, hospitalization, treatment of complications, and follow-up. Measles may cause fever, cough, conjunctivitis, and a characteristic rash, but it can also lead to pneumonia, severe dehydration, inflammation of the brain, and other complications. The risk is particularly serious for infants, pregnant people, and individuals with weakened immune systems. When patients or caregivers miss work, schools close temporarily, or responders are diverted from other duties, the economic effects extend beyond direct treatment costs. The $5.4 million estimate is therefore not a price tag for clinical care alone. It reflects the combined value of labor, services, time, and resources used to control the outbreak and manage its consequences. Because the analysis focused on a defined outbreak and included the costs documented by investigators, the estimate may not represent every possible downstream effect. At the same time, it provides a concrete measure of the scale of resources required to contain measles once transmission begins in a community. Discover more Health Conditions Biological Sciences Finance public health Medical Facilities & Services The findings highlight the economic role of routine vaccination coverage. Measles-containing vaccines train the immune system to recognize the virus before exposure, reducing the number of susceptible people available to sustain transmission. When coverage is high, imported infections are less likely to produce large outbreaks because transmission encounters immune individuals more often. When immunity gaps develop, however, a single infection can trigger extensive contact tracing, emergency vaccination, public communication, and medical evaluation. Maintaining vaccination coverage can therefore function as both a clinical intervention and a form of outbreak-cost prevention. The New Mexico experience also demonstrates why preparedness is central to viral disease control. Public health agencies need surveillance systems capable of detecting suspected cases, laboratories able to confirm infection, trained personnel who can conduct rapid investigations, and clear channels for communicating with the public. The study’s authors argue that these capacities, together with strong vaccination programs, can help communities avoid the substantial health and economic consequences associated with measles. The outbreak’s estimated cost underscores a broader lesson in infectious-disease science: preventing transmission before a virus gains a foothold is often far less disruptive than responding after spread has begun. news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTHCARE Measles Add Topic Ohio measles outbreak grows again, 2026 cases match 2025 total Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Aug. 6, 2026Updated Aug. 7, 2026, 8:12 a.m. ET Hear this story Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 has pushed this year's case count to 45 cases across 10 counties. Tuscarawas County added new cases to its recent outbreak, and Wayne and Trumbull counties are reporting new cases, per the Ohio Department of Health. Ohio reported 45 measles cases in all of 2025. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, surpassing the total from the previous year. Health officials attribute the rise in cases to declining vaccination rates, which have fallen below the 95% threshold for herd immunity. Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues to grow, spreading to several new counties and equaling the total number of cases from 2025 at the last count. Wayne and Trumbull counties are now reporting cases, their health departments recently announced. And the Ohio Department of Health has added cases in Holmes and Knox counties as of Aug. 6. Tuscarawas has confirmed additional cases as of Aug. 5, bringing its total to eight. Statewide, the ODH is reporting 45 cases in 10 counties, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Aug. 6. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Nationwide, measles cases nationwide hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula: 7 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Geauga: 13 Holmes: 1 Knox: 1 Ottawa: 1 Trumbull: 2 Tuscarawas: 8 Wayne: 2 The latest case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with 45 in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Where are measles cases spreading? The Wayne County Health Department reports both its cases are likely associated with a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. One of the Tuscarawas cases is from the same event, that health department reports. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. In Trumbull County, health officials reports that infected individuals were at the Walmart in Liberty on July 29 and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department in Boardman on Aug. 2, during the time they were able to spread the virus. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine ahead of back-to-school season. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. Tuscarawas County added new cases to its recent outbreak, and Wayne and Trumbull counties are reporting new cases, per the Ohio Department of Health. Ohio reported 45 measles cases in all of 2025. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, surpassing the total from the previous year. Health officials attribute the rise in cases to declining vaccination rates, which have fallen below the 95% threshold for herd immunity. Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues to grow, spreading to several new counties and equaling the total number of cases from 2025 at the last count. Wayne and Trumbull counties are now reporting cases, their health departments recently announced. And the Ohio Department of Health has added cases in Holmes and Knox counties as of Aug. 6. Tuscarawas has confirmed additional cases as of Aug. 5, bringing its total to eight. Statewide, the ODH is reporting 45 cases in 10 counties, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Aug. 6. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. WATCHREAD MORE TRUMP NEWS Health expert offers safety tips as measles cases continue to rise in Pennsylvania by Anna Licastro Thu, August 6, 2026 at 5:14 PM Updated Thu, August 6, 2026 at 5:16 PM Health expert discusses rise in measles cases 0Comment Share topics: Measles Pennsylvania MMR Vaccination Public health Penn State Department of Health Vaccine dashboard CENTRE COUNTY, Pa (WJAC) — As measles cases become a growing concern across the state, experts are encouraging the public to take precautions to help stop the spread. While case numbers are still low, experts are emphasizing that measles can be very severe, which is why you should take steps to protect yourself and your community. RELATED | DOH: Measles cases reported in Centre, Jefferson as statewide infections total 200+ “One of the concerning things about measles is that it can be transmissible for 4 to 5 days before you even start showing symptoms. That’s one of the reasons it transmits so quickly is because people don’t even know they’re sick yet,” explained Matt Ferrari, director for the Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics at Penn State. Ferrari says that the measles virus is typically seen more in children, partially due to the fact that many young kids have not had both doses of the MMR vaccine. Powered By 10 519 0 Health expert offers safety tips as measles cases continue to rise in Pennsylvania Share Next Stay “The disease is more severe in children, causes severe fever which can also lead to swelling and inflammation of the brain which can cause neurological complications.” In addition to fever and other common illness symptoms, the virus often presents with a severe uncomfortable rash. Ferrari also says that having measles can make you more susceptible to secondary infections later on, including pneumonia. While the virus is highly contagious, experts emphasize that is also very preventable. Ferrari says that getting vaccinated against measles is by far the most effective way to protect yourself and those around you. “Your vaccination protects not only you, but it protects the others in your community. Again, keep in mind that there are children who could be susceptible to measles but are too young to get the vaccine. There are members of our community that are immuno-suppressed and can’t get vaccinated and they’re still at risk of measles. Our choice to get vaccinated protects us as well as protecting all of those folks.” The Pennsylvania Department of Health created a dashboard on its website to track measles cases, as well as vaccinations. In the past three months, the DOH says its staff have given more than 17-hundred vaccine shots. TBS Report 02 August, 2026, 06:45 pm Last modified: 03 August, 2026, 09:29 am Infographic: TBS An investigation by the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b) has found no genetic evidence that the measles virus circulating in Bangladesh has evolved to reduce the protection offered by the existing vaccine, easing concerns amid the country's worst measles outbreak in years. The preliminary findings, released today (2 August), also identified infants younger than nine months -- too young to receive the first routine measles-rubella (MR) vaccine dose -- as the hardest-hit age group. The findings come as the outbreak continues to spread. According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), four more children died from measles and measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours until 8am today, raising the combined death toll since 15 March to 844, including 748 suspected and 96 laboratory-confirmed measles-related deaths. During the same reporting period, 1,022 new suspected and 115 laboratory-confirmed cases were recorded, taking the cumulative totals to 130,083 suspected and 16,295 confirmed infections. Since the outbreak began, 112,620 suspected patients have been hospitalised, of whom 108,283 have recovered. Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel Infants most affected To investigate concerns that the virus had mutated, researchers from icddr,b and Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute (BSH&I) studied 341 children aged up to 14 years admitted with suspected measles between 20 April and 21 May. Laboratory tests confirmed infection in 324 children. Children aged three to eight months accounted for the largest affected group, with 137 confirmed cases. Researchers grouped the children by age and vaccination status. Among 146 infants below nine months, 142 (97%) tested positive. Among 126 vaccine-eligible but unvaccinated children, 122 (97%) were positive. Of 48 children who had received one vaccine dose, 44 (92%) tested positive, while 16 of 21 (76%) who had received both recommended doses were confirmed with measles. Researchers stressed this does not mean 76% of all fully vaccinated children contract measles, as the study involved only hospitalised children already admitted with suspected infection. The lower positivity among vaccinated children is consistent with vaccine protection, although a population-based study is needed to measure vaccine effectiveness during the outbreak. "The size of this outbreak has understandably raised concerns about whether the vaccine is still working. Our findings provide no evidence that the virus has escaped vaccine protection," said Dr Noorjahan Maliha, associate scientist at icddr,b's Virology Laboratory. She said the hospital-based investigation cannot provide a population-level estimate of vaccine effectiveness, while the 16 infections among fully vaccinated children require further investigation. No evidence of vaccine escape Researchers conducted phylogenetic analysis of 55 whole-genome sequences – 18 sequenced by icddr,b and 37 by the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR). All belonged to the B3 genotype, which has also caused outbreaks in several other countries. Although four mutations were identified in the virus's H protein, researchers said they have been reported previously and do not indicate resistance to vaccine-induced immunity. Window of vulnerability The findings also highlight a vulnerable window for infants. In Bangladesh, the first routine MR vaccine is given at nine months and the second at 15 months. Before receiving the first dose, infants rely partly on maternal antibodies and community protection created through widespread vaccination. An analysis of stored samples from 16 mother-child pairs found maternal measles antibodies declined rapidly, with no protective antibodies detected among children aged three to eight months. "Vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent measles and reduce the risk of severe illness," said Dr Mustafizur Rahman, senior director of icddr,b's Infectious Diseases Division. He called for investigations into why such a large outbreak occurred despite high reported vaccination coverage. Dr Kamrun Nahar, assistant scientist at the Virology Laboratory, said authorities also need to determine why children miss vaccination and whether national coverage masks communities with significant immunity gaps. analysis.time: Publication date: 02 August 2026; Event period: 15 March 2026 to 02 August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Bangladesh; affected population includes infants younger than nine months, vaccine-eligible but unvaccinated children, and hospitalized pediatric cases.
analysis.event: icddr,b released preliminary findings on 02 August 2026 confirming no genetic evidence that the circulating measles virus in Bangladesh has evolved to reduce vaccine protection, addressing concerns during the country's ongoing measles outbreak.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cumulative totals as of 02 August 2026: 130,083 suspected measles cases (16,295 laboratory-confirmed), 844 deaths (748 suspected and 96 laboratory-confirmed measles-related), and 112,620 hospitalizations with 108,283 recoveries. Infants aged three to eight months accounted for 137 confirmed cases, and 97% of infants under nine months tested positive. Among fully vaccinated children, 76% of those hospitalized tested positive, though this does not reflect population-level vaccine effectiveness.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: icddr,b and partners conducted phylogenetic analysis of 55 whole-genome sequences (B3 genotype), identifying four mutations in the H protein previously reported and not indicating vaccine resistance. Researchers emphasized the need for population-based studies to measure vaccine effectiveness and investigate immunity gaps despite reported high coverage. Authorities are urged to determine why children miss vaccination and address potential community-level immunity gaps.

analysis.brief_en: Bangladesh’s International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research (icddr,b) announced on 2 August 2026 that genetic sequencing of measles virus samples from the ongoing outbreak shows no evidence of vaccine escape, easing concerns that the virus may have mutated to reduce vaccine effectiveness. The preliminary findings, based on 55 whole-genome sequences of the B3 genotype, identified four previously reported mutations in the H protein that do not indicate resistance to vaccine-induced immunity. The outbreak, the country’s worst in years, has sickened 130,083 people and killed 844 since mid-March, with infants under nine months—too young for vaccination—disproportionately affected. While 76% of fully vaccinated hospitalized children tested positive, researchers caution this reflects hospital-based sampling and not population-level vaccine failure. Authorities are urged to investigate immunity gaps and reasons for missed vaccinations despite high reported coverage.

The outbreak, the country’s worst in years, has sickened 130,083 people and killed 844 since mid-March, with infants under nine months—too young for vaccination—disproportionately affected. While 76% of fully vaccinated hospitalized children tested positive, researchers caution this reflects hospital-based sampling and not population-level vaccine failure. Authorities are urged to investigate immunity gaps and reasons for missed vaccinations despite high reported coverage.

news.content: YouTube No evidence of vaccine escape by measles virus: icddr,b study Latest Bangladesh Business World Sports Opinion Politics Diplomacy More E-Paper ☀️ 🌐 English বাংলা Russian Hindi Chinese Trending US-Iran Talks Gold Price Measles Outbreak Trump Iran War × Today's Newspaper Latest World Cup Magazine 2026 Election 2026 Follow Us Print: 07 Aug 2026 Health No evidence of vaccine escape by measles virus: icddr,b study Daily Sun Report, Dhaka Published: 02 Aug 2026, 08:41 PM Updated: 03 Aug 2026, 01:57 AM Share Share options Print Copy link Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin A A Preliminary findings from an icddr,b investigation have found no genetic evidence that the measles virus circulating in Bangladesh has escaped the protection provided by the existing vaccine. According to a press release issued by icddr,b on Sunday, the investigation, conducted jointly with Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute (BSH&I), involved 341 children aged up to 14 years who were admitted to Bangladesh Shishu Hospital & Institute with suspected measles between 20 April and 21 May. Laboratory testing confirmed measles infection in 324 of them. The findings showed that children who had received both recommended doses of the measles-rubella vaccine were less likely to test positive for measles than those who were unvaccinated or had received only one dose. Among 146 infants below nine months of age, who were not yet eligible for routine vaccination, 142 tested positive for measles. Of 126 children old enough to be vaccinated but who had received no dose, 122 tested positive. Among 48 children who had received one dose, 44 tested positive, while 16 of the 21 children who had received both recommended doses tested positive. The researchers cautioned that these figures should not be interpreted as showing that 76% of fully vaccinated children contract measles, as the investigation included only children who had already been admitted to hospital with suspected measles. They said the progressively lower positivity rate among fully vaccinated children was consistent with vaccination providing protection, although a larger population-based study would be needed to determine vaccine effectiveness during the outbreak. Genetic analysis found that the circulating virus belongs to the B3 genotype, which has been associated with outbreaks in several other countries. icddr,b conducted phylogenetic analysis of 55 whole-genome virus sequences, including 18 sequenced by icddr,b and 37 by the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR). The analysis showed that all viruses belonged to the B3 subclade and were closely related to strains reported elsewhere, with no evidence that the virus had evolved to evade vaccine-induced immunity. Researchers identified four mutations in regions of the virus's H protein recognised by antibodies. However, they said similar mutations had previously been reported in measles viruses circulating in other countries and that their presence does not indicate resistance to the vaccine. Further laboratory studies are needed to determine whether the mutations have any measurable effect on antibody protection. The investigation also highlighted a period of vulnerability among young infants before they receive the first routine measles-rubella vaccine at nine months of age. An initial analysis of stored samples from 16 mother-child pairs from an earlier icddr,b birth cohort found that maternal measles antibodies declined rapidly during the first months of life. However, researchers said the sample size was too small to draw definitive conclusions and that further investigation was required. "The size of this outbreak has understandably raised concerns about whether the vaccine is still working. Our findings provide no evidence that the virus has escaped vaccine protection. We observed lower positivity among children who had received both doses, although this hospital-based investigation cannot provide a population-level estimate of vaccine effectiveness," said Dr Noorjahan Maliha, associate scientist at the Virology Laboratory of the Infectious Diseases Division at icddr,b. Dr Mustafizur Rahman, senior director of the Infectious Diseases Division at icddr,b, said vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent measles and reduce the risk of severe illness. He said further research is needed to determine why the outbreak became so widespread despite comparatively high reported national vaccination coverage and whether immunity gaps exist in some communities. Dr KamrunNahar, assistant scientist at the Virology Laboratory, said studies would also examine why some children miss vaccination and help refine Bangladesh's immunisation strategy. icddr,b Executive Director Dr Tahmeed Ahmed said the organisation had initiated a broader research programme to investigate why some vaccinated children became infected, factors contributing to severe disease and death, the role of malnutrition, and the decline of maternal antibodies in infants. In response to the outbreak, icddr,b has launched a clinical cohort study across four divisional hospitals, expanded laboratory and genomic surveillance, an enlarged birth-cohort immunology study, a pilot study on zinc alongside standard measles treatment, and community research into why children miss vaccination. The researchers urged parents and caregivers not to delay routine measles-rubella vaccination and to ensure that children receive all recommended doses in accordance with the government's immunisation programme. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-02; event period 20 April–21 May 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Bangladesh; study population: 341 children aged ≤14 years admitted to Bangladesh Shishu Hospital & Institute with suspected measles.
analysis.event: icddr,b, in collaboration with Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, conducted a laboratory-confirmed investigation concluding there is no genetic evidence that the circulating measles virus has escaped vaccine-induced immunity.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among 341 suspected cases, 324 were laboratory-confirmed measles; 142 of 146 infants <9 months (not yet eligible for vaccination) tested positive; 122 of 126 unvaccinated children tested positive; 44 of 48 children with one dose tested positive; 16 of 21 children with two doses tested positive. Circulating virus is genotype B3, closely related to strains in other countries, with no evidence of vaccine escape; four H-protein mutations detected but not associated with reduced vaccine protection.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: icddr,b and partners are expanding genomic surveillance, launching a clinical cohort study across four divisional hospitals, enlarging birth-cohort immunology studies, piloting zinc adjunct therapy, and conducting community research on missed vaccinations; researchers emphasize that vaccination remains the most effective prevention and urge adherence to the national two-dose schedule; further population-based studies are needed to quantify vaccine effectiveness and explain outbreak spread despite high reported coverage.

analysis.brief_en: A study by icddr,b, in partnership with Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, has found no genetic evidence that the measles virus currently circulating in Bangladesh has escaped protection from the existing measles-rubella vaccine. The investigation, which analyzed samples from 341 hospitalized children with suspected measles between 20 April and 21 May 2026, confirmed measles in 324 cases. Among infants under nine months—too young for vaccination—142 of 146 tested positive, while 122 of 126 unvaccinated children and 44 of 48 children who received only one dose tested positive. In contrast, 16 of 21 children who had received both recommended doses tested positive, indicating lower positivity among fully vaccinated children. Genetic analysis showed the virus belongs to genotype B3, with no evidence of vaccine escape despite the detection of four mutations in antibody-recognized regions of the H protein. Researchers caution that these hospital-based findings cannot estimate population-level vaccine effectiveness and call for larger studies to understand why the outbreak spread despite high national coverage. icddr,b has launched expanded surveillance, cohort studies, and community research to refine immunization strategies and address immunity gaps.
analysis.summary_en: A study by icddr,b, in partnership with Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, has found no genetic evidence that the measles virus currently circulating in Bangladesh has escaped protection from the existing measles-rubella vaccine. The investigation, which analyzed samples from 341 hospitalized children with suspected measles between 20 April and 21 May 2026, confirmed measles in 324 cases. Among infants under nine months—too young for vaccination—142 of 146 tested positive, while 122 of 126 unvaccinated children and 44 of 48 children who received only one dose tested positive. In contrast, 16 of 21 children who had received both recommended doses tested positive, indicating lower positivity among fully vaccinated children. Genetic analysis showed the virus belongs to genotype B3, with no evidence of vaccine escape despite the detection of four mutations in antibody-recognized regions of the H protein. Researchers caution that these hospital-based findings cannot estimate population-level vaccine effectiveness and call for larger studies to understand why the outbreak spread despite high national coverage. icddr,b has launched expanded surveillance, cohort studies, and community research to refine immunization strategies and address immunity gaps.

news.content_zh: icddr,b 与孟加拉国 Shishu 医院和研究所合作进行的一项研究发现,没有任何遗传证据表明目前在孟加拉国流行的 麻疹病毒 已逃脱现有 麻疹-风疹 疫苗 的保护。该调查分析了2026年4月20日至5月21日期间341名疑似麻疹住院儿童的样本,确认了324例麻疹病例。在 9 个月以下的婴儿中(对于 疫苗接种 来说太小),146 名儿童中有 142 名检测呈阳性,而 126 名未接种疫苗的儿童中有 122 名以及 48 名仅接种一剂的儿童中有 44 名检测呈阳性。相比之下,接受两种推荐剂量的 21 名儿童中有 16 名检测结果呈阳性,表明完全接种疫苗的儿童中阳性率较低。遗传分析显示该病毒属于B3基因型,尽管在H蛋白抗体识别区域检测到了四个疫苗,但没有证据表明疫苗逃逸。研究人员警告说,这些基于医院的研究结果无法估计人群水平的 疫苗 有效性,并呼吁进行更大规模的研究,以了解为什么尽管全国覆盖率很高,但 疫苗 仍会传播。icddr,b 启动了扩大的 监测、队列研究 研究和社区研究,以完善免疫策略并解决免疫差距。

analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 341例疑似病例中,324例为实验室确诊的麻疹;146 名 <9 个月婴儿(尚未符合 疫苗接种 资格)中有 142 名检测呈阳性;126名未接种疫苗的儿童中有122人检测结果呈阳性;48 名接受过一剂疫苗的儿童中有 44 人检测结果呈阳性;接种两剂疫苗的 21 名儿童中有 16 名检测结果呈阳性。循环病毒为B3基因型,与其他国家的毒株密切相关,没有疫苗逃逸的证据;检测到四个 H 蛋白 突变,但与降低的 疫苗 保护无关。

news.content_title: Wayne, Trumbull counties each report 2 confirmed measles cases tied to Ohio outbreak
news.content: Wayne, Trumbull counties each report 2 confirmed measles cases tied to Ohio outbreak - Two more counties in Northeast Ohio, Trumbull and Wayne, have reported confirmed cases of measles as the statewide outbreak continues. Two more counties in Northeast Ohio are reporting measles cases as the statewide outbreak continues. On Wednesday, health officials in Trumbull and Wayne counties each announced two confirmed cases of measles. Last week, the Ohio Department of Health announced a measles outbreak in the state amid cases in Ashtabula and Tuscarawas counties. On Tuesday, health officials in Geauga County announced five measles cases. WAYNE COUNTY According to the Wayne County Health Department, both of their confirmed cases are "likely associated" with a previously announced measles exposure at Smokey Lane Stables in Sugarcreek on July 17. "The individuals were exposed during the event and later developed symptoms consistent with measles," the department stated in a release. "Other people from other communities were also exposed and contracted measles at this event." Wayne County health officials add that an additional "suspected case" is being investigated as of Wednesday afternoon. "We are actively monitoring Wayne County residents who may have been exposed. We are asking residents to be aware of symptoms and to take precautions when seeking treatment," advised Wayne County Health Commissioner Nicholas Cascarelli. "Without a doubt, being vaccinated against the measles virus still offers the best protection. It is safe and it works." TRUMBULL COUNTY The Trumbull County Combined Health District said it is working with the Ohio Department of Health and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department to investigate potential exposures and identify anyone who may have been exposed. According to the health district, one of the individuals visited the following locations while contagious: - Walmart, 200 Goldie Road in Liberty Township, on July 29. - Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department, 6505 Market St. in Boardman, on Aug. 2. Health officials said anyone who visited those locations and is not vaccinated against measles, is unsure of their vaccination status or has developed symptoms after possible exposure should contact a healthcare provider. The health district recommends that unvaccinated individuals monitor themselves for signs and symptoms of measles for 21 days after any possible exposure. Last week, the Ohio Department of Health announced a measles outbreak in the state amid cases in Ashtabula and Tuscarawas counties. On Tuesday, health officials in Geauga County announced five measles cases. Symptoms of measles include a high fever, cough, runny nose, watery eyes and a rash that typically develops three to five days after other symptoms begin. Officials said measles is highly contagious and can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. People can spread the virus from four days before a rash appears until four days after it develops. The Trumbull County Combined Health District also announced two upcoming measles vaccination clinics: - Thursday, Aug. 6: Mesopotamia Township Hall, 8800 state Route 534, from 9-11 a.m. and 1-3 p.m. - Tuesday, Aug. 11: Trumbull County Combined Health District, 194 W. Main St. in Cortland, from 9-11 a.m. and 1-3 p.m. Residents who believe they have measles are urged to stay home, avoid contact with others and call their healthcare provider before visiting a medical office or hospital so appropriate precautions can be taken

news.content: News Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Ohio's latest measles outbreak doubles with new cases Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Aug. 5, 2026Updated Aug. 6, 2026, 6:50 a.m. ET Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with the total number of cases rising to 11 with seven new cases reported. Some infected individuals may have visited a horse sale in North Bloomfield while contagious. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, a trend experts attribute to declining vaccination rates. The best way to protect against measles is through the MMR vaccine, which is 97% effective after two doses. Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 is growing, with cases more than doubling amid new reports from two counties. Geauga County is reporting five new cases related to the ongoing measles outbreak, defined as three or more related cases, Geauga Public Health announced on Aug. 4. And the Tuscarawas County Health Department reports another two cases as of Aug. 4, and is awaiting laboratory confirmation on more. Previously, the Ohio Department of Health reported four infected individuals — three in Ashtabula County and one in Tuscarawas County — ranging in age from 4 to 30. This brings the total number of cases in the current outbreak to 11. The six cases in Ashtabula and Tuscarawas were among unvaccinated individuals, ODH and the county health department report. The Geauga health department did not list the vaccination status of its five cases. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Nationwide, measles cases nationwide hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991, USA TODAY reports. Geauga County measles outbreak may have spread at a horse sale Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The health department is working with the individuals and their healthcare providers to identify others who may have been exposed, who will be notified by their local health department and provided guidance on quarantining. ODH is working with Geauga Public Health to follow up on potential exposures and promote opportunities for vaccination. The Tuscarawas health department reports that one if its new cases was exposed to measles at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on July 18. The other was exposed during a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. Tuscarawas County cases range in age from 15 months to 19 years. Measles cases in Ohio growing According to the ODH Summary of Infectious Diseases dashboard's last update on July 31, the state was reporting 15 total measles cases and two previous outbreaks – three cases in Cuyahoga County in January and seven cases in Franklin County in February. That total does not include the Geauga cases or any others that may have been reported. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with 45 in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine ahead of back-to-school season. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. analysis.time: Published 2026-08-05; event period July 17–August 5, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Ohio, USA; affected counties: Ashtabula, Tuscarawas, Geauga; exposures linked to Bloomfield Horse Sale (North Bloomfield) and Smokey Lane Stables (Sugarcreek); age range 15 months to 30 years.
analysis.event: Ohio’s third measles outbreak of 2026 is growing, with cases more than doubling to 11; reported by Geauga Public Health and Tuscarawas County Health Department; confirmed by laboratory testing.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 11 confirmed cases; no deaths reported; exposures at livestock venues; 6 of 11 cases in unvaccinated individuals; nationwide U.S. measles cases at 35-year high (2,295 cases Jan–Jul 2026); risk of severe complications including pneumonia and encephalitis.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Contact tracing and exposure notifications underway by local health departments; vaccination promotion by Ohio Department of Health (ODH) and Geauga Public Health; ODH urges MMR vaccination; vaccination coverage in Ohio kindergartners 91.5% (2023); herd immunity threshold (>95%) not met; status: ongoing investigation with pending confirmations.

analysis.brief_en: Ohio’s third measles outbreak in 2026 has more than doubled to 11 cases after seven new reports from Geauga and Tuscarawas counties, the state health department confirmed on August 5. Six cases occurred in unvaccinated individuals, and exposures were linked to a horse sale in North Bloomfield and a stables event in Sugarcreek. Nationally, U.S. measles cases have reached a 35-year high with 2,295 infections reported so far in 2026, driven by declining vaccination rates that have eroded herd immunity. Local health departments are conducting contact tracing and notifying exposed persons to quarantine, while state officials emphasize the 97% effectiveness of two-dose MMR vaccination. No measles-related deaths have been reported in Ohio during this outbreak.

Nationally, U.S. measles cases have reached a 35-year high with 2,295 infections reported so far in 2026, driven by declining vaccination rates that have eroded herd immunity. news.source_body_en: Ohio’s third measles outbreak in 2026 has more than doubled to 11 cases after seven new reports from Geauga and Tuscarawas counties, the state health department confirmed on August 5. Six cases occurred in unvaccinated individuals, and exposures were linked to a horse sale in North Bloomfield and a stables event in Sugarcreek. Nationally, U.S. measles cases have reached a 35-year high with 2,295 infections reported so far in 2026, driven by declining vaccination rates that have eroded herd immunity. Local health departments are conducting contact tracing and notifying exposed persons to quarantine, while state officials emphasize the 97% effectiveness of two-dose MMR vaccination. No measles-related deaths have been reported in Ohio during this outbreak.

news.content_title: Measles case confirmed in Holmes County
news.content: OHIO — The Holmes County General Health District confirmed Tuesday that it was notified of a laboratory-confirmed case of measles in a resident. Currently, the health district is working to identify potential exposure sites and encourage vaccination. Anyone who is identified as potentially exposed will be contacted by public health officials and given guidance on next steps. Last week, the Ohio Department of Health announced the state’s third measles outbreak of this year. So far in 2026, there have been 15 confirmed measles cases. The state had 45 cases in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Nationally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 2,318 cases so far this year, already surpassing the number of infections for the entire year of 2025. Measles, which is extremely contagious, is spread through sneezing and coughing. The virus can live up to two hours in the air where the infected person coughed or sneezed. Once breathed in, an individual can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Symptoms include: - Rash - High fever - Running nose - Cough - Loss of appetite - Red, watery eyes The CDC recommends all children to get two doses of the MMR vaccine — the first dose at 12 through 15 months of age, and the second dose at 4 through 6 years of age. Adults who are unvaccinated or don't know if they received the vaccine can also get one. CDC data shows that vaccination rates for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Ohio are below the benchmark of the recommended 95% by health officials, as they say 95% vaccination rates in a community can help develop herd immunity to a disease

news.content: Son of ex-Tenafly councilman sentenced in child porn case | Exclusive News Bergen Sports HS Sports Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Measles surging across the country; does NJ have any cases? Juan Carlos Castillo USA TODAY NETWORK Aug. 4, 2026Updated Aug. 5, 2026, 7:30 a.m. ET There have been nearly 2,400 confirmed cases of measles in the U.S. this year, the vast majority of them associated with one of the 37 measles outbreaks reported this year, according to the latest numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). In comparison, there were only 285 cases in 2024 and 59 in 2023. U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is now saying that parents should vaccinate their children against measles. Here's what to know about the disease in New Jersey: Are there measles cases in New Jersey? Utah, South Carolina, Virginia, Florida and Texas have the highest number of confirmed cases this year, accounting for roughly 1,900 cases out of the close to 2,400 reported this year. Utah leads with 524 cases. New Jersey is among the states with the fewest cases. According to the CDC, there has been only one confirmed case in the state so far this year. Can adults get measles? Any person that is not immune to the virus can get measles regardless of age. Measles infection tends to be more severe in children under five, pregnant women and adults over 30. What is measles and how does it spread? Measles is an airborne viral illness considered one of the world’s most contagious diseases. It can lead to severe complications and death, particularly in children under 5 and pregnant women. As an airborne virus, it spreads through tiny nasal and throat droplets in the air and on surfaces after those who are infected sneeze or cough. Once the virus is in the air or on surfaces, it can remain active for up to two hours. What can parents do to minimize risk of measles? Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent measles. The vaccine comes in two doses that are usually administered before age 2. If your child is infected with measles, keeping them well-nourished and providing vitamin A supplements can reduce the risk of complications, according to the World Health Organization. Washing hands often and using N95 facemasks can reduce the risk of contracting measles, according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. The measles vaccine is considered safe and affordable and often is combined with immunization for mumps and rubella. Juan Carlos Castillo is a New Jersey-based trending reporter for the USA Today network. He covers weather, and national events focusing on how they affect New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware. supplementary_news.content_title: Lehigh Valley confirms 1st measles case amid nation’s worst year for virus in decades
supplementary_news.content: Health officials this week confirmed the Lehigh Valley's first measles case amid a rise in infections across Pennsylvania and the United States. St. Luke's University Health Network announced Monday night it is treating its first case of the highly contagious disease in recent memory. It is a pediatric case, the network said. "Measles cases are on the rise in the United States, but we now have our first case here in the region," Dr. Jennifer Janco, a St. Luke's pediatrician, said in a video update released by the network . St. Luke's spokesman Sam Kennedy clarified Tuesday the network is treating two patients with measles, both pediatric cases in Lehigh County of siblings who tested positive. One was receiving inpatient treatment, and the other was recovering at home. The infections come as Pennsylvania experiences an increase in measles cases , bringing a national health concern to local communities. Health officials are now urging residents to check their vaccination status and get vaccinated if needed. Janco, chairwoman of the St. Luke's Pediatric Department, emphasized the serious nature of the virus. "Measles is one of the most contagious diseases that we know of. You only need to be around the airspace, not the person, and it can linger in the air," she explained. The virus poses a significant threat to unprotected individuals, Janco said: "Nine out of 10 people who aren't protected are going to contract measles if they're exposed." The disease can lead to severe health complications requiring hospitalization. Janco warned that measles can cause swelling of the brain and affect the lungs. The risks extend beyond immediate illness, as the virus can create ongoing health problems for survivors. The number of measles cases in the U.S. in July surpassed the record-breaking tally for all of 2025 , with five more months of 2026 still to come. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it logged 2,318 cases of measles as of July 23. The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the worst year for measles in more than three decades. Now, 2026 has easily become the U.S.'s worst year for measles since 1991, as major outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona have sickened hundreds and smaller clusters of cases sparked in other states. A Pennsylvania Department of Health dashboard of measles infections statewide shows 176 cases as of Monday, including the two in Lehigh County and seven in neighboring counties — three in Montgomery and four in Berks. Despite concerns of an outbreak, health officials stress that measles is preventable through vaccination. The cases are affecting children in the region, but Janco pointed to an effective solution. "The good news is we can prevent measles cases. So, yes, we are seeing cases in children, but we have a very powerful prevention tool in the form of vaccination," she said. St. Luke's advises parents with unvaccinated children to contact their pediatrician immediately to schedule vaccinations. Many adults may also need protection, and the health network urges certain adult populations to verify their vaccination status. "People born between 1963 and 1967 may have had an older version of the vaccine and might benefit from today's updated version," Janco explained. Additionally, adults vaccinated during childhood may not have received adequate protection. "If you were vaccinated before 1991, you may have only received one dose because that's what the recommendation was then," she said. The current medical recommendation calls for two doses of the measles vaccine. Janco stressed the effectiveness of the complete vaccination series. "We know two doses of the vaccine is a powerful protection tool and we are not seeing cases of measles in vaccinated persons," she said. Those unsure about their vaccination status should consult with their healthcare provider to determine if they need vaccination or additional doses, health officials stressed. Lehigh Valley Health Network, part of Jefferson Health , is also on the alert for measles, with a spokesperson telling lehighvalleylive.com: "The Pennsylvania Department of Health notified us of two confirmed cases of measles locally, following the evaluation of a patient at Lehigh Valley Reilly Children's Hospital. "Appropriate precautions were implemented as soon as measles was suspected, and we will continue to work closely with state health officials." The Associated Press contributed to this report. The Collection Riverpark mall in Oxnard (above) includes Cinemark Century Riverpark movie theater, one of the locations visited by the individual who was later positively diagnosed with measles. | Credit: Drewrx/Wikimedia Commons A case of measles in an individual who had been traveling internationally was announced on August 5 by Ventura County, the county just south of Santa Barbara. Identifying information is not available due to medical privacy rules, but Ventura’s public health contact tracers put together a list of places the individual was known to be before being positively diagnosed: • July 26: Subway, 1941 N. Rose Ave., Suite 600, Oxnard (approx. 8 –10 a.m.) • July 27-August 1: Hacienda Furniture and Mattress, 3200 S. Saviers Rd., Oxnard • July 31: Cinemark Century Riverpark, 2766 Seaglass Way, Oxnard (approx. 7:30 p.m.–midnight) • August 1: Walgreens, 1801 N. Rose Ave., Oxnard (approx. 9:30–11 a.m.) • August 2: Kaiser Permanente, 4949 Market St., Ventura (approx. 9–11 a.m.) With measles, it can take a week or two before symptoms appear, which at first are usually a high fever, cough, runny nose, and watery eyes. A rash starts about 3-5 days after those symptoms appear, generally at the hairline and descending from there. Measles is a highly contagious virus that spreads through airborne particles brought up by coughing and sneezing. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves a room. Ventura County has strong vaccination rates, said the county’s public health officer, Dr. Uldine Castel, and hasn’t had a measles case since 2017. Similarly, Santa Barbara County has a greater than 95 percent measles vaccination rate and has not had a measles case since 2019. People who have been vaccinated or were born before 1957 are generally considered at a low risk. The risk increases for those who’ve never had measles, have not been vaccinated, or are immunocompromised. Anyone at the locations listed and at those times should watch for symptoms, Ventura County advised. If measles is suspected, call before going to a healthcare provider to notify them of the potential for infection. supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC More from ABC Close menuABC ABC News ABC iview ABC listen Kids & Students Indigenous Information & Services news iview listen Loading ABC News Just In For You Politics World Business Analysis Sport Lifestyle Entertainment Quizzes More Search News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ABC News News Home RFK Jr says children should get measles vaccine amid US outbreak ShareShare article RFK Jr says children should get measles vaccine amid US outbreak Topic:Vaccines and Immunity Posted Mon 3 Aug 2026 at 3:49pmMon 3 Aug 2026 at 3:49pm Mon 3 Aug 2026 at 3:49pm Robert F Kennedy Jr is known for his scepticism about vaccines, but says kids should get the measles jab. (AP: Jose Luis Magana) In short: US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr says parents should vaccinate their children against measles. The advice from the longtime vaccine critic comes amid the worst outbreak in 35 years. What's next? International health officials will meet later this year to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has urged parents to vaccinate their children following a record-breaking measles outbreak in the United States. Mr Kennedy, a longtime vaccine critic who has regularly told Americans they should not take medical advice from him, warned people to get the jab during a heated interview on CNN on Sunday, local time. “Parents should get their children vaccinated for measles," he said. "A measles vaccine is effective, it stops measles in about 97 per cent of the cases. People should get vaccinated.” The rise in measles, declared essentially eradicated in the US a quarter of a century ago, has been linked by medical experts to slumping immunisation rates, a trend many attribute in part to vaccine scepticism espoused by Mr Kennedy. More than 2,370 cases of measles have been confirmed in the US this year, already breaking last year's multi-decade high. RFK Jr defended his handling of the measles outbreak in the interview with Dana Bash. (Supplied) During the CNN interview, Mr Kennedy was asked if he took any responsibility for the measles surge. “Absolutely not,” he said. Mr Kennedy later went on to accuse CNN host Dana Bash of "repeating like a parrot" and becoming "flustered". Worst year for measles in decades Many health officials have cited a public backlash to the government's pandemic response and blame Mr Kennedy's anti-vaccine policies for further undermining trust in immunisations. "The whole thing about 'vaccines have been tested and there's been this determination made' is just a lie," Mr Kennedy said in a 2025 interview. The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the most since 1991. This year there have been major outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah and Arizona, as well as smaller clusters in other states. International health officials will meet in November to determine if the US and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. The US eliminated the local spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but in recent years they have fallen below the 95 per cent coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Measles cases under-counted Public health departments and disease researchers have long acknowledged that official counts of disease cases are incomplete because not everyone seeks treatment. Measles testing was conducted in Texas in 2025 (Reuters: Sebastian Rocandio) Experts suspect the spread of measles cases may be wider than has been reported due to the decline in vaccination rates. National vaccination rates for measles, mumps and rubella — which dropped to 92.5 per cent among kindergarteners in the 2024-25 school year, from 95.2 per cent in 2019-20 — obscure even lower rates in certain communities. In Utah, where public health officials have fought measles for more than a year, the virus has struck more than 700 people during that time, according to the state health department. Experts relying on mathematical modelling and genetic analyses indicate that a large outbreak on the Utah-Arizona border could be three to four times bigger than what is known, according to Utah state epidemiologist Leisha Nolen.
